#75467. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

📅 26 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1279 w)

This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1279 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Newly introduced research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.
  • The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.
  • Both measures were linked to mortality risk and indicated similar ability to predict it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newly introduced research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and indicated similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

It has been revealed that it included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

It has been revealed that to measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

Industry observers note that for free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

It has been revealed that from this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:.

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

The average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

The study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own showed modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, remarked that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

“Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”.

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, mentioned that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

“It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she stated. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” noted Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she said.

Theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he remarked.

In a recent development, “And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” said Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he remarked. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have concerns with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

In a recent development, “I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being important,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

Breaking: Ginger Rogers at Home: 10 Photos of the Golden Age Icon’s Glamorous SoCal Life

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1463 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While most people race to the hospital to give birth, Ginger Rogers’s mother, Lela, insisted that her baby girl’s first breaths be taken in their Missouri home.
  • According to recent reports, decades after her death in 1995, Rogers is poised to return to the substantial screen by way of Sabrina Carpenter, who’s set to portray the late actor in the forthcoming, yet-to-be-titled Fred Astaire biopic.
  • Industry observers note that after Rogers separated from her second husband, actor Lew Ayres, in 1936, she and her mother moved in together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While most people race to the hospital to give birth, Ginger Rogers’s mother, Lela, insisted that her baby girl’s first breaths be taken in their Missouri home. “The little four-room house at 100 Moore Street was the perfect choice” for the future icon’s July 1911 welcome to the world, Rogers concluded in her 1991 memoir, Ginger: My Story. The star would go on to live with her extended family in Kansas City at 3306 Bellefountain Street; with her stepfather in Fort Worth at 1510 Cooper Street; and once she became a Hollywood sensation, a sprawling Beverly Hills estate. That joy and sense of peace she found in her childhood residence became a defining feature of her California pad. “It was a fun house, a happy house,” Rogers told Architectural Digest in 1994. “I was never angry when I didn’t have to work, because I liked to stay home so much.”.

According to recent reports, decades after her death in 1995, Rogers is poised to return to the substantial screen by way of Sabrina Carpenter, who’s set to portray the late actor in the forthcoming, yet-to-be-titled Fred Astaire biopic. Tom Holland will star as Astaire. Read on for a glimpse inside the Oscar winner’s off-set life in the places she cherished most.

Rogers on the diving board in 1938.

Industry observers note that after Rogers separated from her second husband, actor Lew Ayres, in 1936, she and her mother moved in together. “I asked Mother if she would like me to build her a house, and if she did, could I live in it with her,” Rogers wrote in her memoir. “The next day she scoured the area for a suitable place to build. She found a wonderful lot high in Beverly Hills on 2.75 acres on Gilcrest Drive in Coldwater Canyon. It had a view that didn’t stop; when the fog burned off late every afternoon, it was possible to see Catalina.” Rogers is pictured at the stunning estate in this 1938 photo.

The actor with her home ice cream fountain.

The Swing Time star added many personal touches to the home, one of which was an elaborate soda fountain. In this 1940 photo, she’s shown whipping up a sweet treat. In her memoir, Rogers recalled all the amenities she installed. “The building took over a year because of labor strikes and material shortages,” she wrote. “When the house was finished, it proved to have been worth waiting for. It had everything I wanted or needed in a house: swimming pool, tennis court, projection room, and my very own soda fountain. Who could ask for anything more?”.

Rogers opened her home tennis court to championship hopefuls so they could get practice matches in.

In a recent development, rogers was an avid tennis player. Though she’s pictured here in 1950 at her Malibu beach house, the actor also had a home court installed at Gilcrest Drive. “On the way to the pool and tennis court were eight sculptured bay leaf trees. Next to the blue-tiled pool was my tennis court. This was my pride and joy,” she wrote in Ginger: My Story. With the knowledge that Rogers had the only en-tout-cas court in the area, the Tennis Association “begged” her to invite young hopefuls for some practice before they went on to championship matches at Forest Hills, New York. “I was delighted to open my court to competitors like Pancho Gonzales, Gussie Moran; and, later, Billie Jean King, Jennifer Hood, and Alice Marble slammed a few over the net too,” Rogers said.

Rogers was known for hosting her Hollywood star friends at home in Beverly Hills.

According to recent reports, the Top Hat actor’s Beverly Hills abode was also a hot party spot for Rogers’s A-list friends. “My home was made for entertaining and I gave party after party,” she wrote in her memoir. “Most of them were informal. I’d serve spaghetti and we’d play some night tennis. Alcohol was never served, just cold drinks. One, a mixture of finely crushed ice, 7-Up, and concentrated orange juice, was a real favorite with the tennis crowd.”.

The star had a close relationship with her mother, Lela.

Rogers loved living with her mother, with whom she’s pictured in the circa 1940s portrait on the piano in this 1954 image. The triple threat pushed back against the term “stage mother” in Architectural Digest; she considered her mom to be “my guide and my professor… she was my encyclopedia. She knew what route to take: She helped Lucille Ball along hers too, you know. It would have been hard to have a career without her.” About their Beverly Hills pad, she added, “we both liked the look of a French farmhouse. And I wanted certain specific things: a helpful bath, a tennis court, and my own projection room, where we had eight or ten director’s chairs, so that friends could come over to watch movies.”.

Rogers with a furry friend at home in the 1950s.

Recent findings suggest that the home featured a main house with bedrooms for Rogers and her mom, as well as a guesthouse for visitors. “The house was very bright,” she told Architectural Digest. “I don’t like dark things; even in my clothing, I prefer to be light and colorful—Springtime for Henry has always been my motto,” she explained, referencing the 1934 comedy. In her memoir, Rogers added, “The style was an American farmhouse with Dutch doors opening to cool breezes. The large bay window in the corner of the living room had a view of Beverly Hills and a bit of Los Angeles. Off the living room was a patio for barbecuing on a flagstone area under a beautiful Australian pepper tree. It was a wonderful place to entertain on crisp California nights.”.

Rogers’s home also included a solarium, and bedrooms with scenic views. “On a lower level was an outside entrance to the playroom,” the actor noted in her memoir. “This room had big windows and comfortable cushions as did the solarium in the hallway to the patio. I read many a book, with apple in hand, buried in those downy cushions.” About her bedrooms, she added, “There were two bedrooms leading from the solarium, one for Lelee [her mother] with a four-posted bed and one for me. My room looked out on the view of Beverly Hills, and I had a beautiful hand-carved mantel for my fireplace.”.

Rogers at work on an oil painting.

Sources indicate that in addition to the stage talents for which she became a star, Rogers was also a painter. Her guesthouse also doubled as a studio. “My studio, which could double as a guesthouse, held all the paraphernalia of my hobbies: painting materials, canvases, paintbrushes, turpentine, pencils, and so on,” she wrote in her memoir. “Whenever there was a lull on set, I’d take out my pencil and sketch,” Rogers added. “I had been drawing for a long time and it seemed to come naturally to me. I found it challenging and relaxing. I never studied drawing or painting, I just did it.”.

In a recent development, in her memoir, Rogers recalled a time when she brought her paintings out for a gallery show. “When I’m not working or traveling, my main source of relaxation comes from my painting,” she wrote. “Gallery owners have wanted to have a one-person show of my work, but I never had the time to organize my paintings. Well, now was the time. Gregg Juarez, a gallery owner and friend of mine, arranged for a show and sale at his gallery in Palm Desert. As we were hanging the paintings for display, I realized these were my children—I couldn’t sell them! Gregg told me I had to sell a few so the customers wouldn’t get mad. I managed to put a few up for sale, but couldn’t part with the rest. So now they are joyously hung in my home for all to see.”.

Rogers was 83 years old when she died in 1995 at home in California.

Industry observers note that rogers remained at her home on Gilcrest Drive until 1970, when her mom urged her to sell while she was away working in Europe. “I had been renting it out more than living in it lately, and Mother thought it was financially sound to put it on the market,” the actor wrote in her memoir. “Besides, she said it needed a newly introduced roof! She handled all the details of the sale…. This was one time I’m not sure Mother knew best. I adored that house on Gilcrest Drive and have regretted selling it ever since.” Rogers died decades later, on April 25, 1995, at her home in Rancho Mirage, per the Los Angeles Times.

The Best Foot Baths for Soothing Tired Feet, According to Podiatrists

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • As a longtime distance runner, my feet can get pretty roughed up after a grueling workout—even with the proper running shoes.
  • A good foot soak at the end of a long day or workout can do wonders for your mental health, too, ultimately supporting your overall health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As a longtime distance runner, my feet can get pretty roughed up after a grueling workout—even with the proper running shoes. But since I don’t have the time or endless funds to regularly hoof it to my local spa for a foot massage or pedicure, a home foot bath is my go-to. The best foot baths allow you to soak your tired toes, with extra features like bubbles, jets, and massage functions to help your feet feel rejuvenated.

A good foot soak at the end of a long day or workout can do wonders for your mental health, too, ultimately supporting your overall health. But unsurprisingly, a lot of the potential perks from home foot baths revolve around your feet. These baths can help boost circulation in your feet and combat inflammation that could lead to pain, swelling, and overuse injuries if it’s left unchecked, says Bradley Schaeffer, DPM, a podiatrist and foot surgeon specializing in sports medicine in New York City. Plus, now that we’re at peak cozy season, shopping for a great foot bath for yourself or a loved one (it’s a great gift for her!) is a cost-effective way to give your feet some R&R.

Doing foot baths a few times a week can help to slough off dead skin that builds up quickly, leaving you with softer, less grody-looking feet, claims Melissa Lockwood, DPM, a podiatrist at Heartland Foot and Ankle Associates in Bloomington, Illinois.

Industry observers note that not all foot baths are created equal, and it’s important to choose one based on your needs. So, if bubbles make you feel uncomfortable (me, hi), a foot bath that simply swirls around warm water may be more your speed. We also tapped Schaeffer, Lockwood, and Suzanne C. Fuchs, DPM, a podiatrist at Luxe Podiatry in Jupiter, Florida, for their advice on what to look for when shopping for these foot health-supportive devices and to get their feedback on their favorites.

According to recent reports, using that guidance and our personal experience, we found factors like size, weight, and additional features matter when choosing a foot bath. At baseline, a foot bath is a container to hold water to soothe your feet. But there are plenty of specific features to keep in mind when shopping for a foot bath.

It has been revealed that the Hospan Collapsible Foot Spa packs a lot of features into a device you can fold flat. A huge highlight is the eight groups of massaging balls that go to work to ease pressure on the bottoms of your feet. (These aren’t motorized, but you can run your feet over them for a soothing effect.) While it’s a good idea to start out with warm or hot water, the Hospan Collapsible Foot Spa has temperature adjustment, allowing you to ramp up the heat between 95 and 118 degrees Fahrenheit without having to toss in more liquid. An LED display keeps tabs on the water temperature, giving you real-time information on how hot it is.

As the name suggests, this foot bath is collapsible and drops down when it’s not in use, making it easy to slide into or under tight spaces. A few potential downsides to consider: Hospan’s bubbles aren’t the strongest you’ll find, and this is a pricier bath when it’s not on sale, although it’s usually marked down a few times a year. But if you’re looking to pamper your feet with a range of options and are okay with investing a little extra, this is a solid choice that will hold up well and does just about everything.

Read More: Best Stress Relief Gifts.

It has been revealed that it’s hard to find a foot bath that checks all the boxes, but the Conair Soothing Pedicure Foot Spa Bath comes really close. This bath allows you to get a good soak with a few extras to take your experience to a newly introduced level. “This model features massage settings, which can enhance relaxation,” Fuchs indicates.

Industry observers note that this bath has a modest price tag of $30, which is significantly less than some others you’ll come across. It also uses vibration for a massage and has a pinpoint massage tool in the center in case you want to work on a particular area of your foot. While there’s no bubble feature, not everyone is into bubbles (they tickle my feet, which isn’t my favorite).

Sources indicate that conair’s foot bath is easy to use and clean, and offers plenty of opportunities to pamper your feet. The Conair Soothing Pedicure Foot Spa Bath uses a toe-touch control to turn the vibration settings on and off, although there’s no remote. This bath isn’t powerful enough to heat up cool or room temperature water, but it does a solid job of keeping already-warm liquid at the same temperature.

Not every foot bath has a bubble feature, and some are stronger than others. If bubbles are a priority for you, Fuchs recommends the Homedics Smart Space Elite Foot Bath. “Known for its bubbling action, this foot spa provides a soothing experience,” she claims.

In a recent development, the bath delivers plenty of bubbles, along with heat, to create a spa-like feel while you soak. It also has three pedicure attachments that pop into the center: a massager, brush, and pumice stone. Those attachments neatly fit into on-board storage when they’re not being used. An ergonomic footbed with massaging bristles on the bottom of the bath also helps cushion your soles while you rest. The whole thing folds up pretty small, and has a special locking system for when it’s filled up.

In a recent development, if you’re interested in a foot bath that will give you a shiatsu-type massage, this isn’t it. But if you love the idea of blissfully scrolling on your phone while your feet are surrounded by warm, bubbly goodness, the Homedics Smart Space Elite Foot Bath is the right choice.

Read More: Best Acupressure Mats.

Getting the temperature just right in your foot bath can be tricky. But the Sharper Image Spa Haven Foot Bath has temperature control, allowing you to punch in the level of heat you want up to 108 degrees and let it go to work for you. This foot bath is loaded with features, including separate bubble and heat options, and free-spinning massaging rollers on the bottom that allow you to control the pressure and speed. (The rollers are removable for cleaning.).

In a recent development, the bubbling action is delivered in your choice of four speeds, and there’s also a removable pumice stone to help get rid of calluses and dead skin. When you’re done with your foot bath, just open the drain plug to let the water seep out. The only major downside to this foot bath (besides the high price) is that it’s not collapsible. But that also means it’s sturdy enough to rest your feet on the side when you want to take a break—a feature you won’t find in baths that break down.

The Medical King Foot Spa has six sets of massaging rollers to help knead out stress and pain after a long day. Couple that with bubble jets, vibration settings, and a built-in heater, and you’ve got a recipe for a good time.

This relatively affordable foot bath comes with a remote control that doubles as a control panel, with clear buttons to adjust the massage mode and flip through three temperature settings as you kick back. You can also set a timer to cut off the features whenever you want. The foot bath is collapsible, so storage under your bed or couch shouldn’t be an problem. This foot bath delivers if you’re looking for a way to work out kinks in your soles without having to put in any major effort.

Read More: Best Compression Boots.

You can splash out on a bunch of different features when it comes to a foot bath, but sometimes you just want a standard soak. If that’s the case—and you want to save some cash, too—consider the Mantello Foot Bath. This barebones bath is as basic as they come, but it has a few features that elevate it above your standard plastic bucket.

The bath has a sturdy plastic design that won’t tip over easily. It’s also deep, giving you plenty of space to soak your calves, too. The base has built-in arch support and raised dots for a little something extra while your feet relax. The open design means it’s easy to clean, too. There are no bubbles, massagers, or built-in heaters. But for a mere $23, what do you expect? If you’re just looking to unwind with a solid soak, this is a great choice.

Recent findings suggest that “Foot baths can offer several benefits for foot health,” Fuchs claims. She lists off a bunch of potential perks, including helping your muscles (and mind) relax, improved circulation, removing the buildup of dirt and bacteria, soothing conditions like athlete’s foot or plantar fasciitis, and exfoliation. Of course, you don’t have to use a foot bath to have good foot health—but many people find that it can be a comfortable way to support it.

Should you use Epsom salts in your foot bath?

Industry observers note that in case you’re not familiar with them, Epsom salts can help soften skin and support muscle relaxation. Fuchs recommends adding Epsom salts or essential oils to your tub to ramp up the relaxation and health perks.

The odds are good that you’ll be hauling a foot bath in and out of a storage spot on a regular basis. Most foot baths aren’t overly heavy, but some higher-tech options have more heft to them than others. (The baths we recommend range from 1 pound to 9 pounds.) Just take a peek at the weight to make sure you can comfortably carry your device around.

Recent findings suggest that if your feet are on the larger side, you want to make sure there’s enough room for them to fit comfortably inside your bath. Also, that foot bath has to go somewhere, both when it’s put away and in use. Check the dimensions and compare them to where you blueprint to use your bath, along with the drawer or closet space where you plan to stash it, to make sure you have enough room.

This came up with every podiatrist we spoke to. “Feet can get gross and we want to be able to have a sanitized bath each time we use it,” Lockwood says. Schaeffer agrees. “Bacteria can grow in these, raising the risk of infections,” he points out. With that, it’s crucial to look for a foot bath that’s easy to clean. That usually means the bath can be disassembled for scrub-downs or at least have very detailed cleaning instructions.

This isn’t a requirement, but having the option to collapse your foot bath can be helpful if you’re short on storage space. Many collapsible foot baths can fold down relatively flat, and have locking mechanisms to keep them in place when they’re in use. But if you have the room, you might prefer the sturdier design of a non-collapsible foot bath.

Many foot baths have features to give you more than a good soak, like bubbles, jets, and massagers. Some will heat up the water for you, and others have helpful elements like remote control, rollers, and pumice stones. These extra features usually come with a higher price, so consider what you will and won’t use if you’re looking to save on a bath.

To choose the best foot baths, I first relied on my own personal experience with these tools, making sure to weed out options I’ve used that have leaked, broken, or just not lived up to the hype. From there, I reached out to three podiatrists located across the country for their feedback on what to look for while shopping for these baths. I also utilized in-house testing by Women’s Health editors for units we got feet into. Each foot bath was evaluated on size, weight, ease of cleaning, and extra features like bubbles and built-in massagers to create the final list. Keeping all of that in mind, these foot baths are worth snapping up to get your soak on.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators notes Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged.

Tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and indicates it has the car’s event data recorder and video. The public was told a car “veered off the road.” It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

Sources indicate that at 11:43 p.m. on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, a 2025 Tesla Model X was heading east on Golden Gate Parkway in Collier County, approaching the Estuary Boulevard intersection, according to a Florida Highway Patrol press release.

The SUV left the road, hit a traffic signal pole on the corner of the intersection, and rolled over. Its passenger, a 50-year-old woman from Fort Myers, was pronounced dead at the scene. The 48-year-old driver, also from Fort Myers, went to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

According to recent reports, FHP said the crash remains under investigation. It hasn’t released the woman’s name, a cause, or anything about speed or impairment. And nothing about a driver-assist system.

Recent findings suggest that under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

Industry observers note that it identifies a 2025 Model X and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged,” meaning Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 39 mph, a collision with a pole or tree, airbag deployment, and damage to the front and the top of the car, which fits FHP’s account of the rollover.

Industry observers note that this record is unusually complete on what Tesla has. It checks the event data recorder, telematics, video, and “other.” And it says Tesla learned of the crash through its own telematics, not just from the media.

Then it redacts the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

In a recent development, how we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 03:41 UTC on October 1, which is 11:41 p.m. in Florida on September 30, two minutes off FHP’s 11:43 p.m. The city, the 2025 Model X, the pole, and the fatal outcome all line up. Because the UTC timestamp crosses midnight, Tesla’s record lists the crash in October, so anyone checking Tesla’s data against September crashes would miss it. It’s the same crash.

Most of the crashes we’ve matched leave real gaps in what Tesla holds. Not this one. Tesla has the video, the EDR, and the telematics, and it knew about the crash on its own.

So Tesla can see what the car did on the approach to that intersection. It knows whether the system steered the SUV off the road or the driver did, whether the car warned him, and how fast it was going when it hit the pole. It filed all of that under a redaction.

It has been revealed that autopilot/FSD might not have caused the crash, but it was active within 30 seconds of the crash, so it’s important to understand what happened. Was the driver distracted? Did Autopilot/FSD make a run move?

Sources indicate that there’s also a living witness here. The driver survived with non-life-threatening injuries, which means FHP can ask him whether he had Autopilot or FSD on and what the car was doing. We don’t know if anyone has. Troopers may not even know Tesla verified the system was engaged.

Sources indicate that this is the second fatal Tesla driver-assist crash in Naples in this NHTSA release. In May, a Model 3 with the system engaged at 71 mph hit an overturned box truck on I-75 at Pine Ridge Road, killing three people. FHP investigated both, and neither crash was ever publicly tied to Autopilot or FSD.

The same release set a new record: 264 Tesla driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236.

In a recent development, this is the cleanest example yet of how much Tesla knows and how little it shares. It detected the crash on its own. It has the video. It has the EDR. A woman riding as a passenger died in a Model X that, according to Tesla, had its driver-assist engaged. And the public account is one sentence: the car veered off the road.

In a recent development, tesla certainly benefits by keeping the information hidden. Most are willing to look past these things and not be suspicious, but ultimately the question is why hide. something if you dont have something to hide.

We’re not saying the system caused this crash. We don’t know, and that’s the point. Tesla does know, and it decided the account of what its car did in a fatal crash is a trade secret.

Industry observers note that if FSD or Autopilot did nothing wrong here, Tesla has the footage to prove it. It was happy to share data in the Katy crash when it helped its case. When Tesla keeps the video sealed, people are going to assume the worst, and Tesla only has itself to blame.

We’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol whether its investigators knew the system was engaged and whether they got Tesla’s video and raw data, or only Tesla’s interpretation of them. Same questions we asked about Vineland. How many more fatal crashes will troopers close without knowing what Tesla knows?

#75462. Does Adversity Hurt Less the Second Time?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1000 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Does Adversity Hurt Less the Second Time?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • My grandfather owned a black World War II winter coat, long and heavy, the kind exhibitionists in movies wear, and in high school and college, I wore it everywhere because it reminded me of this sweet man who would watch Woody Woodpecker cartoons on television with me such that his laugh shook the bed.
  • Nietzsche wrote that what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger, so by his logic, I should have shrugged off my next problem easily.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

My grandfather owned a black World War II winter coat, long and heavy, the kind exhibitionists in movies wear, and in high school and college, I wore it everywhere because it reminded me of this sweet man who would watch Woody Woodpecker cartoons on television with me such that his laugh shook the bed. One night, outside a New York City bar, I realized it was too warm for wool and threw the coat back in my car. When my friends and I came back a few hours later, the window was broken in, and the thief took one thing: my grandfather’s coat.

Nietzsche wrote that what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger, so by his logic, I should have shrugged off my next problem easily. Three psychiatric researchers in Australia borrowed this overplayed line in the title of their scientific article, "What Doesn't Kill You Doesn't Always Make You Stronger: The Impact of Repeated Exposure to Adverse Life Events on Mental Health." Their work addresses questions taken for granted in a sloppy literature on resilience.

Developmental psychologist Ann Masten coined the phrase that resilience is “ordinary magic” in 2001. It has since been dropped into commencement speeches and self-help books, usually shrunk down to the comforting idea that everyone has some. Masten’s own data say something far more precise. She spent years studying homeless families and described their reading and math grades:.

Our studies of homeless families have revealed striking variability within homeless populations, both in the degree of risk and also the level of competence or problems. For example, if one examines individual growth curves for children identified as homeless/highly mobile in the district, the variability becomes evident … Some children show consistent academic resilience, if one defines resilience as average or better reading or math achievement scores, whereas others show consistent problems, covering a range of 5 SD [five standard deviations] or more.

Industry observers note that variability means that some people experience amazing outcomes while others fall apart. Five standard deviations is a spread wide enough to stretch from the bottom 1 percent of the bell curve to the top 1 percent within a group of kids who all lack a stable bedroom. On average, homeless children scored below poor children who had housing, who in turn scored below children who were neither. Masten never noted resilience is a universal human endowment.

According to recent reports, the myth of universal human resilience has a price. If most people bounce back on their own, the logical policy is to leave them alone. They will be fine... eventually.

It has been revealed that asking whether people are resilient is about as useful as asking whether people are tall, because the answer depends on who, measured against what, and when. The better question is what happens when you experience the same difficulty twice and whether the second hurts more or less than the first.

According to recent reports, the Australian psychiatrists studied 23,109 adults who, between 2002 and 2023, experienced adversity. They looked at people who:.

Every year, the same people answered the same question: How much of the time during the past four weeks:.

Scores ran from 0 to 100, which let the researchers compare how far a person sank after a first challenge with how far the same person sank after a second.

Some might say the first time your finances blow up, you can blame bad luck, such as a crooked landlord. The second time, the explanation arrows start pointing at you.

In the study, a first major financial loss lowered scores by 6 to 7 points, the steepest drop of the seven events. A second loss lowered them by 7 to 8 points, and a third hurt about as much as the second—so the harm grew, and then it leveled off.

The people hit repeatedly were poorer to begin with, earning less before their first event. That is, the study highlighted people with tough lives experience terrible events more often. It’s not exactly the most awe-inspiring finding, but it should make us more compassionate. My hypothesis is that a second financial loss comes after the savings account is empty, and you have already asked friends for a loan. By then, you feel incompetent and risk fraying your social ties.

In a recent development, A first theft or break-in lowered scores by about 1 point out of 100—the smallest effect in the study. By those stats, my coat should have been a shrug, and it wasn’t. A question about property crime can’t distinguish a stolen car stereo from my grandfather’s WWII coat. The authors close their paper with the same mentality, arguing that how much an event hurts depends on what the lost thing means to the person and how much is in their psychological arsenal to absorb the pain.

Divorce and serious personal illness or injury both did less harm the second time, so some might offer advice that your second divorce will sting less. As a divorced man, I’m in no hurry to find out, and you shouldn’t either.

A smaller mental health reaction can also mean a person stopped feeling much. For instance, people assaulted three or more times reacted less to each newly introduced attack, and 64 percent of them were women, which unfortunately we know is often a sign of domestic violence.

I want to warn you and everyone you know that emotional numbing should not be misunderstood as resilience or growth.

So did losing my grandpa’s coat make me stronger? Not in the slightest. It was an isolated experience that pissed me off. You, too, have similar one-offs that do not fit tidy little psychological models. Do not assume resilience or breakdowns. Pay attention, ask questions, and listen to better understand the person beside you.

BACK PAIN DOESN'T care about your big intends to sail through life in comfort, making it hard to do everything from getting in a workout to sitting at your computer. Relief can come in many forms, including regularly stretching and strengthening the surrounding muscles, but sometimes, it can also involve using one of the best inversion tables to ease pressure on your back.

In a recent development, “An inversion table is a device that allows you to hang at an angle, or even upside down, with your feet secured,” explains Max Shlykov, MD, an orthopedic spine surgeon at the Maryland Spine Center. “This position stretches and decompresses the spine and surrounding muscles.”.

Sources indicate that it’s important to get this out of the way now: An inversion table won’t magically cure your back pain or fix the underlying cause of it. But it can temporarily ease your pain and the tension that’s contributing to it. Inversion tables tend to be especially helpful for people with chronic back concerns like herniated discs, sciatica, degenerative disc disease, muscle spasms, or general stiffness, according to Shayan Ghadamabadi, DPT, a physical therapist at Michigan State University Health Care Physical & Occupational Therapy.

The best inversion tables are sturdy enough to support your height and weight, with adjustable hanging angles, Dr. Shlykov says. “Models that are more lightweight may be easier on your back to use and set up,” he adds.

You’re not born knowing how to pick an inversion table, making it crucial to choose wisely. Here’s what to consider when looking for one of these pain-relieving tools, plus sturdy options to try. Because you need to know how to actually use one of these tables, we included advice for beginners to help put you on the right path to greater comfort.

It has been revealed that teeter’s FitSpine X3 Inversion Table hits all our best marks thanks to its durability, extended ankle lock handles, and secure, comfortable fit. The device is made with heat-treated steel for unmatched strength and support, and the foam backrest prevents your body from slipping or sliding while inverted, according to Dr. Wallace.

The comfortable table is lined with acupressure nodes to target and release trigger points, and Dr. Wallace says the FlexTech bed moves with your body to enhance decompression and improve range of motion. You can also rest assured about safety features, as the patented wrap-around ankle cups are secure and supportive. Dr. Mesiwala says this is crucial for proper relaxation and effectiveness. What’s more, the lumbar bridge can help release lower back tension and alleviate glute pain triggered by sciatica.

It has been revealed that you’ll also get access to a free personal training app with a library of video and audio guides for on and off the inversion table, Dr. Verma says. The only qualm? It may be difficult or time-consuming to assemble.

It offers a six-position adjustable pin system for safety locking and consistent inversion, a large, padded backrest, and soft-touch foam handlebars for easy access to getting in and out of position, he says. This table is great for anyone, but it’s particularly good for beginners thanks to its ease of use and adjustable headrest, height, and footrest.

This inversion table also features a True Balance System, which helps owners find their center of gravity for smooth, seamless inversion. Not only will this maximize tension release, but it can also improve spinal decompression. Another pro: The headrest is adjustable, too.

When it comes to getting a full, comfortable stretch, the EP-560 is a safe bet. It features patented wrap-around ankle supports, an ergonomic T-grip ankle lock, and an easy-dial foot platform for a more comfortable, secure fit. The backrest is also a game-changer. Most inversion tables use a simple foam material; the EP-560 ComforTrak backrest is designed to reduce friction and enhance spinal stretch and decompression. We also love that it’s pretty customizable. It comes with built-in tools for easy adjustability, including a Lumbar Bridge for deeper traction on the lower back and Acupressure Nodes that target muscle tension.

It has been revealed that the device is made out of an ultra-durable, heat-treated steel, adding an extra layer of strength and support. If you’re a little closer to the 300-lb range, this is a solid option.

It’s on the pricier side, but the Harison Electric Inversion Table is a top pick for both Dr. Mesiwala and Dr. Verma thanks to its adjustable footbed, memory-foam backrest, and heavy-duty build. The device is made with seamless welding and a steel frame to support up to 350 pounds, and the ergonomic ankle lock design is supportive without feeling too tight or restrictive. Security is also a top priority, and the table includes a high-quality safety belt that allows you to strap in while inverted (on top of the secure ankle holders).

The table is heavier than other options on this list, but it’s foldable for easy storage. It also includes a 30-day trial and replacement of spare parts within one year for no extra cost.

If you’re looking for an inversion table that doubles as a massager, here’s your pick. This model has a upcoming, improved ankle-holding system to reduce pressure on the ankles when inverted, while still ensuring a secure, protective fit. There’s also a six-position pin system on the side of the machine that lets you adjust the angle without dismounting the device.

In a recent development, each inversion table accommodates different heights, so it's key to read the fine print. The Teclor Inversion Table adjusts to fit people up to 6'8", making it a good option for taller users. It also can support up to 350 pounds, one of the largest weight capacities you’ll find.

This is a relatively simple inversion table, and the low price supports that. But you’ll still get a comfortably padded back, cushioned handles, and an easy-to-reach handle for adjustability. The ankle-holding system is thickly padded, too. A double-locking system helps to ensure your device is firmly in place when it’s in use. When you’re done inverting, it folds up small enough to stash in a closet.

Sources indicate that consider the Teeter FitSpine LX9 the slightly more luxurious version of our top pick, the X3. This has all the elements consumers love about the X3, including that durable heat-treated steel frame and padded back, but in a slightly sleeker, user-friendly design. The LX9 has an eight-point floating suspension system for a large range of motion, along with reinforced padded handles for a comfortable grip.

Sources indicate that enjoy eight acupressure nodes to help relieve muscle tension while you hang. The included lumbar bridge is adjustable and works to tweak your hip alignment. The LX9 has a step-through design with a specialized boarding platform to make it easy to get on and off. There’s even a built-in storage caddy to hold your gear while you invert.

According to recent reports, using an inversion table isn’t as simple as diving into a latest set of dumbbells. These devices require you to move your body upside-down, making it notable to know what you’re doing and how to ease into the process.

In a recent development, it’s key to start with a “modest” angle vs. going into a full-out inversion when you’re starting out, according to Raymond Agostino, DPT, owner of Agostino Athletics in Fort Myers, Florida. “The goal is to introduce your body to the position and create a gentle traction effect without overwhelming your system,” he notes.

Agostino suggests starting with a gentle recline, like 20 to 25 degrees for 30 to 45 seconds and see how you feel. “If you feel comfortable and don't experience dizziness, increased pain, or other symptoms, you can gradually increase the time or angle over future sessions,” he notes. Agostino recommends only changing one variable at a time—angle and inversion time—to ease yourself in. “You don't need to go farther upside down and stay there longer all at once,” he says.

It has been revealed that when you’re inverted, you may feel a pressure sensation in your head or a mild “head rush,” Agostino claims. “When your head is positioned below your heart, blood pressure and pressure within the eyes can increase, which is one reason inversion feels very different from simply lying flat,” he explains. You might also feel a feeling of fullness in your head or facial pressure. “Those sensations should remain mild and should resolve when you return upright,” according to Agostino.

Agostino points out that you don’t get a trophy for going completely upside down. “If a smaller angle provides the stretch or relief you're looking for, there may be no reason to progress to a full inversion,” he says.

In a recent development, safety is paramount when shopping for an inversion table. "It’s ideal to find a product with comfortable ankle straps and safety locks to keep you secure and in place," notes Kushagra Verma, MD, a board-certified orthopedic spine surgeon at DISC Sports and Spine Center. You also want to make sure the table can be controlled and manipulated by the user if you strategy to use the device alone. Inversion tables should be used with caution, especially if you’re a beginner, says Rahul Shah, MD, a board-certified orthopedic spine and neck surgeon at Premier Orthopaedic Associates. Additionally, older adults and those who have chronic dizziness, high blood pressure, glaucoma, inner ear problems, heart disease, and/or severe injuries should avoid inversion tables without talking to their doctor first, he says. Keep this in mind, too, per Agostino: “A little pressure may be expected. Feeling like something is wrong is not something you need to train yourself to tolerate.” If it feels like your back pain is worsening, or if you develop new numbness, tingling, weakness, or radiating pain, Agostino recommends that you stop using the inversion tale.

Sturdiness and durability are crucial for preventing accidents or instability while you’re upside down, Dr. Verma notes. He recommends always looking for a product made with high-quality materials, such as stainless steel, to provide better support and longevity. Be sure to read customer reviews and seek expert opinions on the machine's sturdiness when shopping. Of course, all the selections on our list have been vetted in this way.

In addition to safety features, all experts agree that it’s crucial to consider how much weight an inversion table can safely hold. (The machine should clearly state this in the product description.) Because the machine puts you in a rather compromising position, maximum weight capacity is key for keeping you safe and at ease, Dr. Shah states. Going over the weight capacity raises the odds that the table will break or flip while you’re on it, potentially injuring you in the process, Agostino says.

It’s crucial to consider the table's length to ensure it accommodates your size and height, indicates Ali Mesiwala, MD, a neurosurgeon and complex spine expert at DISC Sports and Spine Center. Most inversion tables are adjustable for a customized fit, but it’s best to ensure the maximum height is within your range for effective use. The width of the table is another key factor, as a wider table can offer more stability during inversion, particularly if you’re on the taller or heavier side, says Brian Wallace, DC, a chiropractor at Pinewood Family Care. As a general rule of thumb, the width of the table should be wide enough for your core to conformably fit and not fall to either side, Dr. Shah adds.

Sources indicate that depending on your needs, different inversion tables include add-on features like lumbar spine support, heat, memory foam, or massage elements, Dr. Wallace claims. These extra features are not a necessity, but they can be beneficial if you’re looking for added comfort and therapeutic benefits, he says. Just remember: extra add-ons should be considered second to the table's fundamental stability, comfort, and safety.

An inversion table isn’t the cheapest tool you’ll use to reduce your back pain, but there is a range to consider. Most tables will run you anywhere from $150 to $450, with higher-priced models having additional features like heat, memory foam, and massage.

Recent findings suggest that to track down the best inversion tables, Men’s Health editors, including contributor Korin Miller, consulted three orthopedic surgeons, a neurosurgeon, a chiropractor, and two physical therapists to learn more about the notable features to look for in an inversion table. From there, we looked at the most popular inversion tables on the market and narrowed the field based on our experts’ requirements. Each inversion table was ranked based on factors such as size, weight capacity, and safety features. This story was first published in August, and was updated in November to reflect the most recent products on the market, along with advice on how to use these machines.

Extended inversion can cause excessive blood flow to the head and lead to nausea, vomiting, and dizziness, so Dr. Mesiwala recommends using an inversion table for a maximum of five minutes at a time, up to twice a day. If you’re a beginner, he suggests only inverting for 30 seconds once a day as you get your bearings.

The best time to use an inversion table is typically when your muscles are relaxed, such as after a workout at the end of the day, says Dr. Wallace. Remember: You should not be inverted for long periods, and it’s best to start slowly and work your way up to time and frequency.

It has been revealed that this is ultimately up to you. Some people feel comfortable with their arms by their sides or crossed over their chest, while others prefer to stretch them overhead. You can also put your arms on the support bars. Essentially, you should do whatever feels comfortable to you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, hospital ratings have become an notable resource for choosing where to receive care. They influence which doctors patients choose, how far they are willing to travel, and whether they seek care at a different facility.

On October 27, Healthgrades unveiled the recipients of the 2027 Specialty Excellence Outpatient Awards and Specialty State Rankings.

It has been revealed that the annual awards recognize hospitals delivering outstanding patient outcomes in specialty care across the United States. Healthgrades is the leading platform used by Americans for finding a doctor or hospital.

Newly introduced research from Healthgrades highlights that hospital quality is increasingly a factor in healthcare decisions.

According to recent reports, around 80% of patients report that when looking for a doctor, the quality of the hospital where they practice matters. Additionally, 7 in 10 patients (68%) say they’re more likely to seek care for a procedure or health condition from a doctor who works at a hospital with high quality ratings.

What’s more, around 71% of patients say they would switch doctors to gain access to a higher-rated hospital.

“Our specialty awards identify the nation’s top-performing hospitals across numerous medical specialties, helping consumers find high quality care tailored to their specific needs,” said Alana Biggers, MD, MPH, medical advisor at Healthgrades.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

Industry observers note that “Navigating the complex healthcare system can feel daunting, but taking a proactive stance to understand where to access superior care can enhance your healthcare journey and overall experience. The ability to make informed decisions about your health — and where to get care — is a cornerstone of self-advocacy, and we are proud to help make that information accessible to all patients.”.

Healthgrades identifies hospitals that deliver exceptional outcomes across common outpatient procedures and specialty conditions.

Finding high quality care is crucial, particularly amid a growing gap between top-performing and one-star hospitals.

According to Healthgrades, from 2023 to 2025, if all hospitals had performed at the five-star level from 2023 to 2025:.

“One of the biggest challenges is balancing increasing patient needs with the resources available to healthcare professionals,” Biggers noted.

“Hospitals face workforce shortages, growing administrative responsibilities, financial pressures, and increasing complexity in patient care. Physicians and other healthcare professionals need adequate time and support not only to evaluate and treat patients, but also to communicate results, coordinate follow-up care, and address concerns that arise between visits,” she continued.

“When healthcare teams are adequately supported, they are better positioned to communicate effectively with patients, coordinate care, and address patients’ needs.”.

Biggers said that ensuring equal access to quality healthcare is challenging because of factors such as:.

Hospital closures and reduced services make access even more difficult. Biggers identified a few possible solutions, such as expanding outpatient care, building community partnerships, using telehealth when appropriate, and improving coordination among healthcare providers.

“Ultimately, providing high quality care requires more than clinical expertise. It requires healthcare systems to invest in their workforce, strengthen care coordination, and create environments where healthcare professionals have the resources they need to provide safe, effective, and patient-centered care,” Biggers noted.

“Equally vital, healthcare systems must ensure that patients have meaningful access to these services, regardless of where they live or their socioeconomic circumstances.”.

Healthgrades acknowledges hospitals that excel in three aspects of specialty care:.

Biggers remarked that outstanding hospitals recognize that high quality care extends beyond just treating an illness.

“It involves listening to patients, understanding their individual circumstances, and ensuring they feel respected, informed, and involved in their healthcare decisions,” she noted.

Patients want to find a hospital that excels in the procedures or health conditions relevant to them.

The recipients of the Specialty Excellence Awards are among the top 15% of hospitals specializing in these areas.

Healthgrades evaluated patient outcomes at roughly 4,500 hospitals across 31 common procedures and conditions to reach their decisions.

Among the list of Specialty Excellence Award recipients, Healthgrades also recognizes America’s 100 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for 11 specialty areas andAmerica’s 50 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for four specialty areas.

“An outstanding hospital prioritizes both patient care and the people delivering that care,” Biggers told Healthline.

“While clinical outcomes, patient safety, and access to evidence-based treatments are essential measures of quality, I believe hospitals must also invest in workforce development and support. This means ensuring physicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals have appropriate staffing levels, adequate clinical and administrative support, and opportunities for continued professional development,” she continued.

Healthgrades awards U.S. hospitals that excel at Outpatient Orthopedic Surgery, Outpatient Joint Replacement, andOutpatient Prostate Care.

Outpatient care is one of the fastest-growing areas of healthcare. The number of orthopedic procedures performed in an outpatient environment has grown exponentially in recent years.

Recent findings suggest that from 2020 to 2025, outpatient hip replacement procedures grew by 81%, while inpatient procedures dropped by 75%. Outpatient knee replacements increased by 71% while inpatient volumes decreased by 70%.

“I believe several factors are contributing to the growing demand for outpatient care, including advances in medical technology, a greater emphasis on preventive care, and the increasing need to manage chronic medical conditions,” Biggers said.

It has been revealed that “Many services and procedures that previously required hospitalization can now be safely performed in outpatient settings. Patients also appreciate the convenience of receiving care closer to home and avoiding unnecessary hospital stays,” she added.

To meet the increasing demand for outpatient procedures, Biggers cautioned that healthcare systems must ensure that these services are adequately staffed and supported.

“Effective communication and coordination between outpatient providers, specialists, and hospitals are essential to maintaining continuity and quality of care,” she noted.

State Rankings identify the top three or five hospitals in eligible states across 19 key specialty areas.

The rankings are based on clinical performance and build on the 2027 Healthgrades Specialty Excellence Awards Methodology.

State-level specialty care rankings help consumers find outstanding local hospitals for their condition or procedure.

The analysis used Medicare inpatient data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) from 2023 to 2025, and assessed patient outcomes across 31 conditions and procedures.

These outcomes served as the foundation for determining Specialty Excellence Awards and state hospital rankings.

With consumer-facing awards and ratings influencing healthcare decisions, transparency about their methods and limitations remains essential.

Ratings can help patients ask better questions and compare options, but they should complement — not replace — clinical guidance and informed decision making.

This resource includes an overview of how Healthgrades picks award recipients, plus a list of the top U.S. hospitals for specialty care.

It has been revealed that to be eligible for a Specialty Excellence Award, hospitals must receive a rating in the required procedures and conditions used to determine the award. Some awards are based on a single procedure, while others are based on a grouping of procedures. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that last spring, the wildlife center received two likely orphaned turkey poults (young turkeys).
  • Industry observers note that “Since we never raise baby animals alone, we had to find a companion for the remaining poult,” the wildlife center wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It seems straight out of a Disney movie—wild animals from two different species becoming inseparable friends. And yet that’s what happened at the Raven Ridge Wildlife Center in southeastern Pennsylvania, between a turkey and a mourning dove.

Recent findings suggest that last spring, the wildlife center received two likely orphaned turkey poults (young turkeys). To calm them down, the team put them with a feather-duster as a stand-in mother turkey. Because turkey poults are easily stressed, they are difficult to rehabilitate, according to a Facebook post by the wildlife center. In fact, one of them didn’t make it.

Industry observers note that “Since we never raise baby animals alone, we had to find a companion for the remaining poult,” the wildlife center wrote. “We paired it with a baby mourning dove of similar size, hoping they would comfort each other while eating and exploring as they are both ground eaters.”.

In a recent development, the pairing turned out to be a raging success. They formed an inseparable bond that Raven Ridge Wildlife Center had never seen before. Months later, the team gave the dove a soft release, meaning the bird could leave whenever it wanted. But he clearly had no intention of leaving his friend. The dove continued returning to the turkey’s cage, and the two would sit near each other on either side of the separation.

“After a few days, we put the dove back in with the turkey, and it was clear they were happiest together,” the wildlife center explained. But “we knew keeping them caged for the rest of their lives, or keeping them just because they were cute, was neither an option nor fair to these wild animals.”.

In a recent development, as such, the team contacted a large sanctuary in Pennsylvania to request a joint release. This way, the duo could choose whether to stick together or follow their own paths. After their soft release, the dove flew into the trees and the turkey started foraging, free to stick together or join other members of their species.

“We don’t know if they’ll stay together, but our team made sure they had a safe place until they were ready to be on their own,” the wildlife center concluded.

#75455. What a Trillion Dollar Industry Cannot Give You

What a Trillion Dollar Industry Cannot Give You

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1613 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • It has been revealed that two thousand years ago, the Tamil poet Avvaiyar wrote a line that every child in Tamil Nadu still learns: Arithu, arithu, maanidaraai pirathal arithu.
  • I think about that verse every November, and this year more than most.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

It has been revealed that two thousand years ago, the Tamil poet Avvaiyar wrote a line that every child in Tamil Nadu still learns: Arithu, arithu, maanidaraai pirathal arithu. Rare, rare it is to be born human. And then she went further. Rarer still, she said, to be born whole, without the body failing you from the start.

I think about that verse every November, and this year more than most.

In the past month, our team published a randomized pilot trial of yogic breathing and meditation for adults with long COVID, and a study in people living with Parkinson's disease. When you sit with these patients, the suffering is not abstract. A woman in the long COVID trial told our interviewers she had developed “a mental block about breathing because of all the breathing problems.”.

Think about what it means to be afraid of your own breath.

Sources indicate that what we offered them was modest: a few minutes of breathing practice and a guided meditation, taught online, done at home. We did not cure anyone. The data demonstrated that breathlessness eased by a clinically meaningful margin, fatigue and mood improved, and nobody was harmed. Temporary relief. Less anxiety. A way to live more comfortably with a condition that isn't going away.

Sources indicate that and when you see them at one level, you feel something else, which is harder to say out loud. You feel fortunate. You were born, for now at least, without that burden. You have been handed the capacity to experience this life in its full depth, and most days, you forget to use it.

I am a physician scientist, so let me be precise about what we know. Across the published studies from our center, the measures move in one direction. Miracle of Mind, a single seven-minute guided meditation, shifted self-rated affect in 1,325 people, with the largest shifts in those who started lowest. High-density EEG in 103 people highlighted brain rhythms begin to reorganize within two to three minutes of the same practice and peak around seven. Long-term practitioners carry brains that read about six years younger than their chronological age on sleep EEG. And in the long COVID trial, three weeks of practice moved breathlessness, fatigue, and mood against a waitlist control.

None of this is mystical. It is what happens to attention, emotion, and physiology when a person turns inward in a structured way. Meditation has a distinct origin and an enormous body of technical work from India, and it belongs to everyone, East or West. At its core, it raises awareness. And raising awareness is the most reliable tool I know for the stress and anxiety that come with simply being alive right now.

Which brings me to the machines.

Recent findings suggest that we are living through the construction of a trillion-dollar artificial intelligence industry. These systems solve mathematical problems that defeat most of us, and they connect islands of knowledge in ways no single human mind can. They matter. They will make medicine safer, work easier, and life more comfortable, and I use them every day.

It has been revealed that what this industry has really done is put very strong technology into the hands of the common person. A capability that belonged to institutions a few years ago now sits in a teenager's pocket. Some of us may even be over-equipped, holding more power than our habits are prepared for. It is a knife with two edges. At one end, it accelerates learning in ways that would have seemed miraculous to my teachers. At the other, it can be misused, carelessly or deliberately, at a scale we have not seen before.

In a recent development, that makes this the moment to hold the instrument with precise awareness. No regulator, and no model, can do that for the person holding it. It is left to us. And that is why raising individual awareness and individual consciousness is not a spiritual luxury alongside the technology. It is the one investment that keeps pace with it.

Industry observers note that but the machines are not going to give us the human experience. The profoundness we are seeking does not arrive through an interface. It has to come from within. There is no evidence that these systems have such experiences themselves, and we do not know how we would tell if they did. What they can give is comfort. What they cannot give is the goosebumps.

Consider basketball. Analytics tell every team to shoot the three, and on average, the teams that listen win more regular season games. Then the playoffs arrive, and something else takes over. Composure. Fear. The ability to stay present when the arithmetic states you should already have lost. Teams built on the average falter there, because the average was never the game. The same is true of art, of music, of the moment a surgeon's hands know something before the mind does. The human experience is where greatness lives, and it is not a calculation.

The yogic tradition described the mind with a precision we are only now catching up to. It named 16 parts in four categories: buddhi, the intellect that dissects and decides; ahankara, the sense of identity that tells the intellect whose side it is on; manas, the vast silo of memory, running back through evolution; and chitta, pure intelligence, unsullied by memory, the dimension that is simply aware.

A machine can be built to imitate the first three. It can reason, be given a persona, and hold more memory than any of us. Chitta is a different matter. That is the intelligence no one can touch, and it is the ground on which every meditation practice stands.

The same tradition that mapped the mind also told us how to live in it, and the instructions are more practical than people expect.

Sadhguru, my spiritual master, claims: Be a mother to the whole world. That is not sentiment. It is a standard. Absolute inclusion, absolute compassion, extended without first checking whether the other person deserves it. No algorithm optimizes for that, because it is not an outcome. It is a way of being.

Industry observers note that then there is acceptance, which is widely misread as passivity. Consider your work. You may or may not get the promotion you seek or the position you have earned. You have only two choices. Stay, and keep raising your capability until the question answers itself. Or step back, look at the whole picture, and if the picture states so, leave. Both are acceptance. What acceptance rules out is the third option most of us choose: staying and resenting it.

And there is agency. Sadhguru indicates, every action you take is yours. Every reaction, too. The moment you accept that, you stop waiting for the world to arrange itself before you can be well, and you become, in the most literal sense, the author of your own experience.

Inclusion, acceptance, agency. These are enormous pieces of intelligence, worked out over millennia by people who had no instruments beyond their own attention. The machines can remind us of them. They cannot practice them for us. That part, like the goosebumps, is ours.

According to recent reports, so, this Thanksgiving, I am grateful for the things my instruments can measure, and more grateful for the things they cannot. I am grateful to have been born human, and whole enough to sit on a cushion and close my eyes. I am grateful for the patients who do the practice anyway, breath by careful breath. And I am grateful for a tradition that asks me to be a mother to the whole world and gives me the tools to try. Above all, I am grateful for the goosebumps that arrive, unbidden, in nearly every meditation, the surest evidence I have that something here no industry will replicate.

In a recent development, if you have seven minutes this week, spend them with your eyes closed doing the Miracle of Mind. The machines will still be there when you open them. So, I hope you will.
