📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

IN THE TWO weeks since Robert Pattinson’s name was first mentioned in connection with James Bond—and in the handful of days since he was officially cast in the role—I’ve heard lots of talk about him as an actor, and him as a fit playing 007.

These have been some of the easiest conversations I’ve had all year long, because, quite simply, Pattinson has been one of the best actors working for the last decade and counting. While his first big breaks came in the commendable space of films based on YA books (Harry Potter and Twilight), he’s long established himself at this point as an actor who can just about do it all, taking on a mix of projects big and small, characters good and evil. He’s shown a full capability run the full gauntlet from sane and noble to absolutely psychotic.

Sources indicate that but I also recognize that not everyone is grinding out the indies from this year or the hidden gems from that year. Not everyone is even seeing the movies that some of us think of as the huge movies that everyone saw. But James Bond Casting is the kind of news everyone hears. And so I wanted to do my part to make sure everyone knows one thing only: Robert Pattinson rules.

Truly. There’s a common description for many cool actors: “He’s a character actor in a leading man’s body.” And no one seems more true to that than Pattinson, as his jawline cut from marble is often put to work in playing some of the most twisted and eccentric characters you’ll see in any movie. Hell, in 2026 alone, he’s already played a groom-to-be from hell in The Drama, a scheming villain in The Odyssey, and an ambitious 2000s television personality (a.k.a. To Catch a Predator’s Chris Hansen) in Primetime. And that’s not even to mention his role as the villain in Dune: Part Three (from his future Bond director Denis Villeneuve) coming later this year.

In a recent development, but that’s the glory of Pattinson, too—he clearly loves doing all that stuff, but he’s still the dashingly handsome, arrestingly charming guy on the surface, too. It’s a rare combination that makes him a unique star for our times; and clearly the massive studios agree, as he’s now been cast as two of contemporary movie culture’s most famous recurring roles, Batman and James Bond.

Recent findings suggest that he’s got a ton of great movies on his resume, ranging from blockbusters to little-seen independents, and almost all are worth your time. He’s even got small roles in some movies—like when he plays a professional driver for Julianne Moore in David Cronenberg’s Maps to the Stars—where he pops even as he tries to keep things grounded.

But I tried to keep it simple and get you ready for what makes him one of our very best, and a truly inspired Bond pick. So I stuck with six movies. That’s not too bad, right? A six-movie watchlist. Once you watch these six, you’ll get what you need to get about Robert Pattinson—and why he’s both one of the best actors working today, and a slam-dunk pick to play James Bond.

According to recent reports, pattinson went through a complicated process to become Bond that may or may not have involved being paid $1 million just to audition... but you can basically consider his role in Christopher Nolan’s Tenet as his first audition, and one all of us get to see. Nolan’s time-traveling espionage caper is a cool, sleek thriller that’s also a fast-paced battle to keep up with—and Pattinson’s Neil is the cool-as-a-cucumber agent who knows how to keep the whole thing grounded. He’s got great chemistry with the film’s lead, John David Washington, which may even give you ideas on how a Bond and Felix Leiter partnership could work out in a future film. Tenet is an extremely cool movie, and Pattinson is somehow the coolest thing about it.

Also see: Cosmopolis, probably Netflix’s The Take in early 2027.

It has been revealed that while Pattinson has been doing impressive work for basically his whole career (even check out Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire!), it was Good Time—from directors Josh and Benny Safdie—that helped a lot of people in the moviegoing community wake up to just how good he’d become. This million-mile-a-minute crime story follows Connie (Pattinson) as he runs around in the seedy underbelly of Newly introduced York City looking for money to bail him out of one terrible situation after another. In other words... it’s a Safdie movie. If you want to see how a Pattinson Bond could look as he deals with a mission gone awry or some other massive fuck-up, this is your movie.

Recent findings suggest that it’s not easy to put a whole movie on your back—and it’s even harder when it’s something that comes with massive expectations. In 2022’s The Batman, Pattinson became the latest actor to put his spin on Gotham City’s cave-dwelling vigilante, and, in typical Pattinson fashion, made him a character all his own. Where Pattinson shines is in the care he puts into both the Batman and Bruce Wayne personas; his early-career Batman is basically an ass-kicking noir detective, while his Bruce Wayne is kind of a brooding emo rich kid. The whole movie rocks, essentially a three-hour crime epic—but it’s easy to see why Amazon-MGM and director Denis Villeneuve felt comfortable putting their franchise on Pattinson’s bat armor-covered back.

Recent findings suggest that pattinson has also put in a lot of time playing creeps. In The Lighthouse, he plays a man stuck spending time with a grumpy, farting Willem Dafoe, and who eventually falls into his own descent, killing people and seagulls alike. And, well, he’s just not a great guy. Pattinson’s willingness to lose himself in a role, putting that psychosis front and center for all to see, marks an impressive willingness to both not be the hero, and to be vulnerable—which can also be great tools for someone as layered and complex as Bond tends to be.

Also see: The Odyssey, The Devil All the Time.

There’s another hallmark of Pattinson’s recent work: playing characters who, at one point or another, reveal themself to be freaky little freaks. Sometimes, like in James Gray’s The Lost City of Z, that’s evident from the jump, as he plays a bespectacled, bearded oddball. Other times, like in The Drama—which came out earlier this year and was a major hit for A24—he appears to be relatively normal at first, before eventually putting his antisocial behavior or extreme neuroses on display. The Drama is a wonderful character study, with Pattinson and Zendaya bouncing off each other marvelously, and it’s a thrill to watch Pattinson’s devolution into weirdo in a story that feels decidedly of the present. James Bond is a sleek, cool, spy, sure, but you don’t cast Robert Pattinson to just be a sleek, cool spy. Hopefully there’s a way for him to tap into his freak bona fides.

Also see: The Lost City of Z, Probably Dune: Part Three.

If you want to see Pattinson’s ability to be purely magnetic on screen, Primetime is the movie. Director Lance Oppenheim’s narrative debut is a thrilling and darkly comedic portrayal of ambition in the post-9/11 age of mid-aughts TV, and Pattinson leads the way as NBC’s Chris Hansen. He absolutely crushes every aspect of the role, making tens of choices with every single line and eating them all up like he’s at an all-you-can-eat buffet. He also bounces masterfully off costars Merritt Wever and Skyler Gisondo. The character is huge, narcissistic, and borderline evil, but Pattinson’s real skill is on display in making Hanson still never feel quite less than human. That’s a tricky balance beam to walk—but one he always manages to make look effortless.

Industry observers note that the VW ID. Polo Trend with the 37 kWh battery went on sale in Europe in July, starting at just 24,995 euros, or about $27,500, with a WLTP range of 207 miles (334 km).

By mid-September, reports claimed Volkswagen’s entry-level EV was already essentially sold out across actross all trims, with more than 30,000 orders and a 10-month waitlist.

According to the latest update from German automotive news outlet Edison Media, that number has doubled in about two months, and buyers now face delivery times of up to 21 months for the base ID. Polo Trend. Deliveries for the sporty GTI version are expected to be around seven months.

Industry observers note that “We clearly planned too conservatively,” a VW manager told Edison during an interview. While VW expected about 90 to 95% to choose to lease, the leasing rate is only about 50%.

The larger 52 kWh battery version has also seen higher-than-expected demand, while 90% surprisingly opted to buy the optional €810 ($890) detachable towbar.

As a result, the manufacturer is prioritizing higher-margin models, which is likely leading to longer delivery times for the base ID. Polo.

The entry-level variants “just clog up to the line,” Volkswagen’s manager said during the recent interview.

According to recent reports, demand for the ID. Cross, the electric equivalent to Volkswagen’s T-Cross, is also already exceeding expectations.

The 52 kWh battery version will go on sale in the UK this week, starting at £30,260 ($40,000). The ID. Cross Life with the 37 kWh battery will go on sale in January 2027, starting at £26,985 ($35,500).

It has been revealed that volkswagen’s new entry-level electric cars are off to a promising start. The electric urban car family, which includes the ID. Polo, ID. Cross, and the CUPRA Raval and Skoda Epiq, has received nearly 150,000 orders combined since production began in June.

However, the German automaker is still facing an uphill battle. The VW Group posted an operating loss of 5.9 billion euros ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its worst quarterly loss since the Dieselgate scandal.

In September, Volkswagen’s supervisory board approved its Future Blueprint 2030, which calls for reducing its global workforce by up to 100,000, closing plants, and narrowing its vehicle lineup to cut costs.

According to a study by the Institute of Environmental Science and Technology at the Autonomous University of Barcelona and McGill University, people travel an average of 78 minutes per day, regardless of mode of transport or distance covered. That means there’s a possibility of adventure in every bike ride, at each bus stop, and even while waiting in the airport security line. (You never know who will break liquid limits or forget to take their pepper spray off their keyring, giving everyone a delay and a story!) But you may also need accessories to keep the adventure comfortable.

No one knows that better than a friend or family member who is always heading to a new destination (typically very far, in this case). The best travel gifts bring more ease and peace of mind whether someone you know is dealing with 78 minutes’ worth of errands, cross-country travel, or long-haul international treks with a lifetime’s worth of layovers.

Other neck pillows don’t support neck movement in all directions; the Cabeau Evolution X Deluxe is a $70 neck pillow filled with customization to make it “just right,” just like Goldilocks. Change the pillow’s circumference, adjust the top or bottom lobes to change its height, and pull the adjustable cord and ball lock for a fine-tuned fit. Plus, it’s designed to not pull or tangle your hair. It comes in seven color options, including lively options like butter yellow, lavender, and cornflower blue.

Sources indicate that I’ve been a significant proponent of the “fanny pack worn across chest” since way before “crossbody” entered the vernacular. I’ll attach my keys to the strap, throw my favorite chapstick, headphones, and earplugs in the smaller front compartment, and stow my phone, wallet, and passport into the main compartment, which doesn’t eat my belongings like other purses in my possession. Recent findings suggest that the $219 40-Liter Baboon to the Moon Go-Bag is my duffel bag of choice for weekend trips or pet-sitting stints. I’ve gotten my money’s worth out of my baby pink bag, which has been by my side at conferences in Chicago, trade highlights in Nevada, jaunts to Washington, D.C., and Philadelphia for concerts, and train rides to my hometown. Wherever she goes, I follow, thanks to a water-repellent coating, stash pockets, and—best of all—her agreeableness with TSA or gate agents as a carry-on. B2TM (the abbreviated name for the company) added a laptop sleeve and compression straps to its most recent version of the Go-Bag, meaning I can ditch my laptop backpack and pack smarter than ever, AKA: I can shove more crap in there. Don’t be blindsided by overweight luggage with this $10 portable bag scale from travel inspira. It’s easy to use: Switch between tare weight, kilograms, and pounds with the press of a button. I’ve used this $38 BAGGU 3D Zip Set to store extra cords, emergency must-haves like Band-Aids and hand sanitizer, and to keep shoes separate from clothes. Industry observers note that these $40 Matador FlatPak Toiletry Bottles hold 90 milliliters of volume at half the bulk, so you’ll have enough shampoo, body wash, conditioner, and lotion for the entire trip. #75435. Latest Update: Why Your Brain Feels Tired When Your Body Isn't

Latest Update: Why Your Brain Feels Tired When Your Body Isn't

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (746 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • You’re sitting down at your computer to answer one simple email.
  • You read the first paragraph—and re-read it to make sure you got everything.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

You’re sitting down at your computer to answer one simple email.

You read the first paragraph—and re-read it to make sure you got everything. But the second paragraph is harder to read because your attention keeps getting pulled away—to other messages, to your calendar for upcoming meetings, to a text message that just came in.

And even though you can go back to reading your work after that, you find that you can’t remember what you were trying to say in the first place.

According to recent reports, you are not physically tired. You haven’t done any physical activity, and you haven’t left your desk all day. So, why do you feel like your brain is done for the day?

You might have been concentrating, making decisions, solving problems, or switching between tasks. Sometimes, switching between tasks can be the most tiring.

People who experience mental fatigue report thinking slowly, getting annoyed easily, and struggling to focus on a task in front of them.

This form of fatigue causes people to feel like they are at maximum capacity and don’t want to make any more decisions.

The mental fatigue you feel is not all in your head.

In a recent study, 117 adults participated in a randomized crossover design. After 45 minutes of sustained mental effort, in addition to rating their mental fatigue, participants were given a rigorous set of cognitive tests to complete.

After a 45-minute control task of simple work, the same set of tests and ratings were administered.

Furthermore, in addition to the typical decline in performance associated with mental fatigue, the participants completed a set of physical tests of performance that were rated by the participants themselves for how much effort they required and how much exertion they produced.

Effortful mental activity affects perception of physical effort and performance, as shown by Work Time Varying studies (long periods of work with demanding tasks) of 30 to 90 minutes duration, using either computerized tasks and/or self-report.

Results found that within a work period of extended duration, there was an increase in reported fatigue and a decline in performance on reaction time and accuracy tasks.

Also reported was an increase in decline in attentional control with corresponding changes in EEG measures of attentional control.

So there’s actually something going on when you say that your brain is done.

There is one thing called "tired." That name covers a variety of situations, all of them to be dealt with differently.

Mental tiredness is not the same as feeling sleepy (physical tiredness), and physical tiredness (after, for example, having lifted heavy things or engaging in sport) is not the same as feeling mentally tired after a long and stressful day.

Sources indicate that there is a big overlap between these states of fatigue: After a sleepless night, our cognitive functions are affected; and after a long, stressful day, we are tired physically as well as mentally. Yet, they are not the same and must be combated in different ways.

Industry observers note that mental fatigue from task-switching, i.e., alternating focus between different tasks, is a serious distraction from one’s work, and it can feel like a heavy burden. The term "multitasking" is often used to describe such work behavior. However, in reality, the brain isn't doing multiple things at once. Instead, it is constantly shifting attention between different tasks.

According to recent reports, these tasks do not have to feel "dreadful" in order to be detrimental to one’s health. Each task-switch seems to be minor in itself, yet in the end, it leads to a lot of starting and stopping throughout the day. Sitting for long periods of time is, of course, bad, but sitting at a desk all day is not necessarily worse than standing for long periods of time and being on the move all day.

While there is no one-size-fits-all solution to fighting fatigue at work, certain things can help.

Habay J, Arenales Arauz YL, Proost M, et al. Mental fatigue negatively impacts cognitive and physical performance outcomes: A large-scale randomized crossover trial. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2026;58(2):225-241. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000003852.

Sources indicate that zhang C, Liu N, Xu D, Yuan W. Effects of task duration on mental fatigue: A multimodal analysis based on subjective, behavioral, and electrophysiological measures. Int J Psychophysiol. 2026;221:113336. doi:10.1016/j.ijpsycho.2026.113336.

Industry observers note that when it comes to mountain towns, there’s good, there’s great, and then there’s Aspen—so needless to say, Aspen’s hotels are the height of luxury. Among one of the world’s finest ski towns (with a whopping four mountains on one lift ticket), this winter wonderland is rife with dazzling accommodations. The best hotels in Aspen offer everything: luxury spa experiences; fine dining; ski-in, ski-out access; and all the après-ski cocktails you can get your hands on.

It has been revealed that if resort life isn’t quite your speed, fear not—there are plenty of picture-perfect rentals you can snag on Airbnb or Vrbo. Expect a robust selection of spacious condominiums, luxury mountain chalets, and backcountry cabins, most of which are within walking distance from one of Snowmass or Aspen Mountain’s peak-reaching gondolas and ski resorts.

Don’t love the snow? Good thing Aspen is a top-tier year-round destination. Ideal for climbers, equestrians, cyclists, and other adventure-seekers, the Rocky Mountains provide a backdrop for just about any summertime alpine experience you can dream up. The town’s famed Food & Wine Classic in June is also a can’t miss. Each luxury hotel and off-the-beaten-path rental we found offers access to some of the best adventures in the West, whether you visit in January, July, or anytime in between. Consider this your cue to scroll below and book your stay while date availability lasts.

Perks: Daily champagne sabering, full-service spa, heated outdoor pool, multiple on-site restaurants, pet-friendly, valet parking.

For the ultimate choice in old-school luxury, check in to the St. Regis. The grand, chalet-style property sits at the foot of Aspen Mountain—just a five-minute walk from the Silver Queen Gondola—and pairs classic Rocky Mountain charm with five-star hospitality. Inside, rooms are outfitted with buttery leather headboards, fine linens, marble bathrooms, and mountain views framed by mahogany trim, while the hotel’s on-call butler service can handle tasks like unpacking luggage and drawing a post-ski bath. The RAKxa Wellness Spa remains one of the best in town, offering oxygen facials, a heated outdoor pool (perfect for a post-slopes soak), and many more wellness-minded amenities. Still, this grande dame doesn’t take itself too seriously. Since 2023, it’s been home to The Snow Lodge, a winter spinoff of Montauk’s famed Surf Lodge. The après scene here has become the hottest ticket in Aspen—Diplo, Rampa, and Bob Moses have all spun sets in the open-air courtyard—while the group’s latest supper club and nightlife concept brings coastal-cool energy to the Rockies with candlelit dinners, Champagne towers, and late-night dancing under the stars. It’s a rare blend of heritage and hedonism—the kind of place where you can trade ski boots for stilettos without missing a beat. From $649 per night.

Perks: Fitness center, multiple restaurants and bars, in-town transport, heated pool and hot tubs, pet-friendly.

Perks: Ski-in/ski-out, heated outdoor pool, spa and fitness center, airport transfers, concierge desk, complimentary mini bar snacks and soft drinks.

The only AAA Five Diamond–rated hotel in Aspen, the Little Nell blends the best of the West with the cosmopolitan luxuries you’d expect from a five-star hotel. Every detail is dialed in. Guests can unwind at the heated outdoor pool and hot tub, book a treatment at the Little Nell Spa, or rely on the property’s Les Clefs d’Or–certified concierge team, who have a reputation for making the impossible happen (heli-skiing trip to Telluride, anyone?). Food and wine take center stage here, too—the hotel’s Chefs & Somms dinners pair Michelin-caliber cuisine with rare vintages from a 20,000-bottle cellar, one of the most impressive in the Rockies. But it’s on the mountain where The Little Nell truly shines. The Ski Concierge team can arrange first tracks before the lifts open, snowcat powder tours, or private gear fittings in your room, ensuring you’re perfectly prepped with your helmet and bindings. From $800 per night.

Perks: Rooftop hot tub, lobby bar and restaurant, pet-friendly, EV charging.

In a recent development, for a quieter boutique experience, you’ll want to stay at Mollie Aspen. Opened in late 2023, the hotel blends Japanese and Scandinavian design, creating an atmosphere that feels immediately restorative. Roomy plush leather chairs, well-worn rugs, custom woodwork, and a plethora of unique design accents welcome weary travelers and exhausted skiers, exuding the type of vibe you’d expect from a well-loved and hard-to-reach mountain chalet. Despite the tucked-away vibe, Mollie’s location couldn’t be more central—you’re steps from downtown’s galleries, the Aspen Art Museum, and cultural landmarks like the Aspen Institute and Wheeler Opera House. If you’re too tired for a jaunt downtown, the Mollie also has a lobby restaurant and poolside rooftop bar where you can while away the hours. The rooftop, in particular, has become a gathering spot for the design-savvy après crowd, offering mountain views and mellow vinyl playlists. From $278 per night.

Perks: All-suite accommodations, outdoor heated lap pool and hot tub, fitness center, tennis and pickleball courts, shuttle service.

Backed up against the Rocky Mountains, Aspen Meadows Resort is a midcentury masterpiece tailor-made for design aficionados. Originally conceived as part of the Aspen Institute campus by artist and architect Herbert Bayer, the property is steeped in Bauhaus principles, with clean lines, geometric forms, and a playful use of primary colors throughout its public and private spaces. Best for art and design nerds, the resort’s 98 suites feature Bauhaus-inspired furnishings, while common spaces include art exhibitions, outdoor sculptures, and West End Social, a recently redesigned restaurant with aspen-wood paneling, Colorado marble, and colorful textiles. Some of the stand-out amenities include a shuttle service with routes into town and the Aspen airport, a heated saline pool and hot tub, and ski butler service. When you’re looking to venture outside of the hotel’s chic walls, there are 40 acres to explore, which include plenty of great sledding hills for those visiting in the winter months and a massive sculpture collection. There’s also the on-site Resnick Center for Herbert Bayer Studies, where rotation exhibitions explore the artist’s legacy. With so much space for playing, there are more activities for visitors than could fit into 10 different trips. Can’t-miss itinerary items include themed scavenger hunts, hot-air balloon rides, fly fishing, snowshoeing, and—of course—lots of skiing. From $359 per night.

Perks: Airport shuttle, pet-friendly, on-site fitness room, rooftop lounge.

For travelers who want to be right in the heart of it all, The Limelight Hotel Aspen offers front-row access to the town’s best shops, restaurants, and bars—plus it’s just steps from the Silver Queen Gondola, which whisks skiers to the top of Aspen Mountain in under 20 minutes. The atmosphere is lively yet low-key, thanks to communal spaces like the buzzy lounge, where locals and visitors gather for wood-fired pizzas, live music, and craft cocktails. The property staff helps guests craft the perfect stay, with activities including hiking adventures, whitewater rafting, art museum visits, and more. Some rooms feature balconies and patios and are draped in mountain charm (think: wool blankets and fireplaces). From $299 per night.

Perks: Mountain view, wood-burning fireplace, fully equipped kitchen, in-unit laundry, hot tub, security system, free parking, housekeeping available for a fee.

In a recent development, just a block from the Silver Queen Gondola, this newly renovated two-bedroom condo makes it easy to spend mornings skiing Aspen Mountain and afternoons exploring the restaurants, boutiques, and après-ski spots in Aspen’s downtown area. Inside, cozy furnishings and a wood-burning fireplace make the living room an inviting place to warm up after a day on the slopes. The two bedrooms offer flexible sleeping arrangements, with a king bed in the primary suite and two twins that can be converted into another king in the second bedroom. The kitchen is outfitted with stainless steel appliances, an induction cooktop, and all the cooking equipment needed to whip up dinner at home, though with Ajax Tavern so close, you might not bother. From $865 per night.

Perks: Heated outdoor pool, fully equipped kitchen, in-unit laundry, pet-friendly, free parking.

There is a lot of architectural woodwork to behold in this modern Aspen condo, but thanks to an abundance of windows, the effect reads bright and airy rather than moody ski lodge. Paneled ceilings, exposed timber rafters, wood floors, and floor-to-ceiling cabinetry bring plenty of warmth to the interiors, while clean-lined furnishings give the two-bedroom space a more contemporary feel. Equipped with one king bedroom and one queen, the condo is particularly well suited to two couples traveling together or a family of four. In the exteriors, the heated pool offers another way to unwind, though the slopes are hardly far away: The property sits just off the Lower Corkscrew run on Aspen Mountain, steps from Lift 1A. From $1,272 per night.

Perks: Mountain views, private patio, soaking tub, in-unit laundry, free parking, pet-friendly, housekeeping available for a fee.

Industry observers note that aspen's Victorian-era architecture is every bit as charming as its mountain scenery, and this one-bedroom apartment near Pioneer Park puts you in the middle of one of the town's most scenic historic neighborhoods. Recently remodeled, the 540-square-foot space has bright, sunlight interiors that includes an open-blueprint kitchen and living room that seems considerably larger thanks to oversized windows lining the walls. A queen bedroom separates guests from the main living area, and modern conveniences like air-conditioning, a dishwasher, and in-unit laundry make longer stays especially comfortable. Although the apartment sits on a peaceful residential street, downtown Aspen's restaurants, boutiques, and the historic Wheeler Opera House are just a short walk away, and a nearby bus stop makes getting to the ski slopes easy. From $391 per night.

Perks: Wrap-around deck, washer and dryer, wood burning fireplace, Wi-fi.

Tucked just behind the St. Regis, this one-bedroom apartment puts you right in the center of Aspen without feeling caught in the crowd. The interiors are warm and functional rather than flashy—a wood-burning fireplace, buttery cotton linens from Garnier-Thiebaut, and plenty of closet space for your suitcases give the space an easy, lived-in comfort. A wraparound deck nearly doubles the footprint, inviting morning coffee in the sun or an après-ski glass of wine with views of the surrounding peaks. Everything is set up to make a stay feel effortless. There’s dedicated parking, air conditioning, and in-unit laundry, plus a Sonos sound system and high-speed Wi-Fi for streaming or working remotely. The open kitchen has all the essentials, while the living room feels like a natural place to gather after a day outside. Professionally managed by Aspen Vacations, guests enjoy thoughtful extras—an invitation to the members-only Caribou Club, and insider tips on local dining and trail access are just a couple to name. Steps from world-class restaurants, boutiques, and the Silver Queen Gondola, this retreat feels equal parts modern pied-à-terre and alpine hideaway—a polished perch for soaking in the best of Aspen, no ski-valet required. From $408 per night.

Perks: Fireplace, free parking, washer and dryer, shared pool and hot tub.

Right on the edge of downtown Aspen, this riverfront condo feels worlds away from the bustle. Floor-to-ceiling windows frame the Roaring Fork River, filling the space with natural light and the sound of rushing water. Inside, the palette is crisp and minimal—soft grays, creamy whites, and natural wood—letting the view take center stage. The open living area flows onto a private balcony, and a sleek kitchen with stainless appliances and stone counters may convince you to eat in. Better yet, there’s some practical touches, like in-unit laundry and high-speed internet, as well as amenities more commonly seen in hotels, such as a shared indoor pool, hot tub, and gym. From $412 per night.

Craving an escape? From colorful carry-ons to cleverly designed packing cubes (how did we ever travel without them?), shop everything you need to make the journey in style—and as streamlined and stress-free as possible.

The 8 Best Home Office Chairs, Approved by Spine Specialists

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

If you work from home, you know how much of a difference the right office chair can make. Take it from someone who's spent five years working remotely and learned the hard way that the couch isn't the best place to spend a workday. Between a standing desk, an under-desk treadmill, and monitors, outfitting your home office can get expensive. But if you're going to splurge on one piece of WFH gear, an ergonomic office chair that supports your back throughout the workday is a good place to start.

Recent findings suggest that “A supportive chair can reduce the risk of lower back pain, neck and upper back pain, poor circulation, and fatigue,” says Kevin Lees, director of chiropractic operations at The Joint Chiropractic. “This may also lead to improved productivity, enabling individuals to stay focused on their tasks without distractions from trying to get comfortable.”.

To find the best home office chairs, our team consulted spine specialists and tested several popular ergonomic chairs for weeks in our own workspaces, sitting for up to eight hours a day. Our favorite is the Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro, which impressed us with its customizable support and easy assembly at a reasonable price compared to premium models from Herman Miller and Steelcase.

In a recent development, the right home office chair will be different for everyone, but there are a lot of factors that will remain the same, like adjustable lumbar support and thick seat cushioning. Keep reading to find which of these eight expert-recommended chairs are the perfect addition to your workday.

Meet the experts: Kevin Lees, Director of Chiropractic Operations at The Joint Chiropractic.Dr. Gbolohan Okubadejo, a spine surgeon and the head of The Institute of Comprehensive Spine Care.

In a recent development, the Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro is our pick for the best home office chair because of its combination of comfort, adjustability, and value. At $499, it’s packed with easy-to-use adjustments that make it a steal. You can customize the seat depth, lumbar support, tilt tension, recline, and more without having to take your eyes away from your work.

After testing the chair for over a month and sitting for four to six hours per workday, WH Digital Designer Taryn Colbert gave it a five out of five, praising how easy it was to assemble and customize. In fact, she found herself using it even when she wasn't working.

Industry observers note that “While I work, I sit it up to work on my posture,” she states. When doing her hair or playing computer games, she reclines the chair into what she calls “lounge mode.”.

The armrests alone offer five types of adjustment, and you can add a headrest or a taller cylinder for an additional cost. While the mesh version has a low-key look, the leather and vegan leather options are worth considering if you want a bit more style.

Colbert’s biggest gripe was the wide wheelbase, which made it difficult to maneuver through doorways and across carpet.

Industry observers note that still, if you’re looking for a classic ergonomic office chair, this model is great for both first-timers and seasoned remote workers. Its customizable design is intuitive enough to use every day without requiring a four-figure investment.

From the iconic Eames Lounge Chair to the ergonomic Aeron office chair, Herman Miller has earned its reputation for making some of the best seats around. At upwards of $1,500, the Aeron is certainly an investment, but you can customize practically everything, from the arm pads to the casters. It’s available in three sizes, with several options for armrest adjustability, back support, and tilt.

WH Deputy Editor Eunice Lucero-Lee tested the medium-size Aeron in the Jasper colorway for two to four weeks, sitting for six to eight hours per workday. Lucero-Lee, who regularly experiences lower back pain, gave the chair a 5 out of 5.

Recent findings suggest that “This had perfect lumbar support for a whole eight-hour day's work,” she says. She also appreciated the adjustable armrests and how smoothly and quietly the wheels rolled while still offering enough traction and control. (The deep forest green colorway was another bonus.).

Sources indicate that instead of a traditional foam cushion, the Aeron features a breathable mesh seat that offers an almost weightless feeling. And the chair arrives fully assembled—as we'd expect at this price point.

While the steep price tag was Lucero-Lee’s biggest gripe, the Aeron’s customizable fit and excellent lumbar support make it a worthwhile splurge if you spend the better part of your day at your desk.

Industry observers note that if you like to lean back and stretch your legs between meetings, the FlexiSpot ErgoX is worth checking out. Beyond customizable lumbar support, seat depth, and armrests, it features an adjustable headrest and a retractable footrest, so you can kick back and put your feet up while catching up on emails or taking a breather between calls.

According to recent reports, WH Fitness Reviews Editor Natascha Grief, who already owns a Herman Miller office chair, tested the ErgoX for over a month, sitting for six to eight hours per workday. While she initially found the back support a little uncomfortable, it took about a week for her to get used to sitting in a more upright position.

In a recent development, “I think a good comparison would be switching to a pair of very supportive/corrective shoes after wearing pairs that are less structured,” she states. Once she adjusted to the chair, she liked the firm back support and how the headrest helped her maintain a comfortable neck position.

In a recent development, grief also loved how comfortable the chair was when fully reclined, though she found the mechanism for pulling out the footrest a little clunky. She ultimately gave the chair a 4 out of 5.

Considering how many adjustments and extras you're getting for the price, the ErgoX is a great option if you prefer a more supportive seat but still want the flexibility to kick back throughout the workday.

Like the Herman Miller Aeron, the Steelcase Gesture comes at a luxury price point, but its sturdy construction, supportive cushioning, and impressive range of adjustments help justify the investment. The chair comes in different materials and colors. Plus you can customize wheels for hard floors or carpet.

Of its many adjustable features, including recline and lumbar support, the most unique is its 360-degree armrests, which allow you to comfortably position your arms whether you're typing on your laptop or scrolling through your phone.

In a recent development, after testing the Gesture for two to four weeks and sitting for two to four hours per workday, WH Managing Editor Laura McLaughlin gave it a 5 out of 5. She loved the firm seat cushion and how the chair managed to feel both stable and flexible.

“The back support specifically feels incredible, with firm yet comfortable padding and adjustable lumbar support,” she indicates.

At nearly 60 pounds, the chair is on the heavier side, and McLaughlin found it surprisingly difficult to roll around. That noted, she felt that its weight contributed to how sturdy and supportive it was.

The Gesture can also support up to 400 pounds, just like the Steelcase Series 2, and is backed by a 12-year warranty, which is reassuring when you're spending four figures on an office chair.

Recent findings suggest that if preserving your home’s interior design is top of mind, then the Branch Verve is minimalist with a unique flair and very comfortable. Made by the same brand as our top pick, this chair is $100 more and has fewer points of adjustment, but it also has a thick seat cushion and a breathable, beautifully designed 3D-knit back that comes in seven chic monochromatic looks.

You can adjust lumbar support, seat depth, and tilt for a decent fit. The chair comes with an optional headrest for $59 more, and the armrests are height-adjustable as well as removable. The chair itself is on the heavier side, weighing in at 40 pounds, but it’s also Greenguard Gold certified, which means it has been tested for volatile organic compounds and chemical emissions.

Read More: Best Standing Desks For Walking Pads.

For those who struggle with back pain, a supportive office chair can be the difference between a productive workday and injury. The Steelcase Series 2 is the best option for those folks because it’s weight-activated—you just sit, and the chair’s back tension adjusts to you.

The thick seat cushion relieves pressure, and you can adjust the height, width, and depth of the armrests. (Most office chair armrests are just adjustable by height and sometimes width.) The chair can also support up to 400 pounds, which is about 100 pounds more than most of our picks. In terms of design, you can choose between a variety of colors, two frame colors, an optional headrest, and wheels for carpet or hard flooring.

Read More: Uplift Kneeling Ergonomic Chair Review.

In a recent development, at under $500, the HON Ignition 2.0 is a budget office chair that still delivers in terms of support and adjustability. The chair itself is lightweight and easy to maneuver at under 25 pounds, and it sports a simple silhouette that won’t be an eyesore in your home office. The armrests can be raised and widened, and you can also easily adjust lumbar, tilt, and seat depth.

It has been revealed that you can also opt to forgo armrests to bring the price closer to $400 or add a headrest and still keep the chair under the $600 threshold. The chair also comes backed by a limited lifetime warranty, which is unique for a high-quality home office chair. (For reference, the warranty on our top pick only lasts for seven years.).

At less than $100, the TikTok-famous Pukami Criss Cross Chair is a great option if you’re furnishing your home office on a budget. The extra-wide, foam-cushioned seat offers plenty of room to sit cross-legged, and its minimalist design and variety of color options make it easy to match with your home decor.

Sources indicate that despite its affordable price tag, the chair swivels, tilts, and can support up to 350 pounds. While it lacks the adjustable lumbar support, armrests, and wheels of our pricier picks, it’s worth considering if you work from home occasionally and don’t want to spend hundreds of dollars on an office chair.

Here are some key features to consider while you search for the best office chair for your body and needs.

Office chairs are not one-size-fits-all, which is why adjustability is crucial. “Adjustability lets the chair match your body so your spine stays in a neutral, supported position,” says Dr. Gbolohan Okubadejo, a spine surgeon and the head of The Institute of Comprehensive Spine Care. The lumbar support should match the curve of your spine, and your feet should be able to sit flat on the floor, according to Okubadejo.

“An unsupportive chair, or one that does not fit properly, can lead to chronic musculoskeletal injuries over time,” Lees notes. “This may lead to pain that persists throughout the day, affecting sleep and stress levels. Long-term injuries may also include nerve damage that can lead to weakness or numbness.”.

Industry observers note that most home office chairs are height adjustable and have armrests that can be raised. If a chair has a headrest, which isn’t essential, that may be adjustable as well. “Being able to tweak depth, tilt, and lumbar support prevents hot spots and improves blood flow during long sits.” Okubadejo says. “Small adjustments through the day break up static strain, so muscles don’t fatigue and posture doesn’t collapse.”.

Lumbar refers to the lower back, and supporting this curve in your spine can relieve disc pressure and keep your pelvis in a neutral position, according to Okubadejo. “Good lumbar support lowers the risk of stiffness and pain during long hours at a desk,” he says.

Like chair height and seat cushioning, lumbar support will vary by person. “Postural muscles start to relax after a few minutes of sitting,” Lees says. “This leads to added stress on the spinal joints and extremity joints.” Luckily, many office chairs allow you to adjust the height and curve of the lumbar support. Okubadejo recommends options that can move up and down as well as in and out instead of stationary lumbar support.

The main components of a comfortable office chair are a sturdy frame, a thick seat cushion, and a supportive, breathable back. Most office chairs these days have a metal or plastic frame with a foam cushion and mesh back, although you can find upholstered and leather versions.

If you have the opportunity to test chairs in person, make sure that the seat is firm enough for you. “If the cushion is too soft, it won’t offer the support needed over time,” Lees notes. “A cushion that is too firm could create pressure points and possibly affect blood flow in the legs.”.

The materials of a chair can contribute to its overall weight and weight limit—both of which are notable to keep in mind during your search.

In a recent development, office chairs, like our top pick from Branch, can be beautiful in their own right but not necessarily as stylish as a sofa or armchair. Unfortunately, you may need to prioritize comfort over design when working from home, but you can opt for chairs with upholstery-like materials or lots of color options to marry the two.

Office chairs range in price from under $100 to more than $2,000, but you’ll find that most quality office chairs will cost around $500. It may seem like a lot to spend on a single chair, but it may also be your most-used piece of furniture outside of your bed and mattress if you work from home.

It has been revealed that as a longtime remote worker and someone who suffers from chronic back pain, I’m particularly passionate about high-quality office chairs. When I set out to find the best home office chairs, I looked for a variety of models that would suit different body types, from height to weight. Supportive office chairs are easily adjustable, especially when it comes to seat height, armrest height, and lumbar support, so I wanted to highlight chairs that delivered on all three and beyond, with a few budget-friendly exceptions.

It has been revealed that my top picks span a wide range of prices, from just $60 to a couple of luxury investment options over $1,500. Whether you’re starting a upcoming remote job or desperately need to revamp your home office, these are the best home office chairs that will keep you comfortable and supported all day long.

Not all commutes are created equal, and tackling a hard commute takes a lot more than a motor and a set of wheels. Ausom knows this better than most, with six highly capable, long-range electric scooters designed to handle your toughest trips. And this Black Friday, you can get the right tool for the job at the lowest prices of the year.

There’s a difference between owning an electric scooter you haul out the farmer’s market every few months and actually riding one every day. If you’re just covering the occasional trip around the neighborhood, almost anything with two wheels and a battery will probably do. But if you’re depending on your scooter to handle a hard commute climbing hills, navigating broken pavement, and covering serious distances ever day, the right equipment matters – and Ausom has the right equipment for just about any ride.

From November 16-December 1, Ausom’s has the right equipment making that decision a little easier this Black Friday, with its entire electric scooter lineup hitting its lowest prices of 2026 and additional savings available exclusively to Electrek readers when they use the code ElectrekFB at checkout.

Before diving into the individual e-scooter breakdowns, let’s first take a look at the flash sale deals available throughout the event. These limited-stock offers will run from 9 p.m. to 10 p.m. EST and cannot be combined with the exclusive discount code or any free gifts.

With six different models on offer this shopping season, Ausom has the right ride for just about every kind of rider, from everyday campus commuters looking for dependable transportation between bells to high-strung adrenaline junkies ready to push the limits of tiny, two-wheeled performance. Here’s the rundown:.

Built for real-world roads, the Gosoul 2 offers smooth, quiet, and confident travel across city streets, wet roads, and light gravel with puncture-resistant 10×2.5″ tubeless tires that reduce the risk of flats, enhance grip, and reduce maintenance needs for everyday dependability. E-ABS brakes cut motor power for faster responses and shorter stopping distances with superior control, while the powerful, 1100W motor, 70 km (~44 miles) of range, and ability to haul riders up 20% grade hills make the Gosoul 2 a great choice for any tech-savvy commuter.

Regularly priced at $729, the Gosoul 2 is on sale this month for just $569, and $549 for Electrek readers.

According to recent reports, for riders who want something more than basic transportation, the L2 Max Dual Motor brings serious performance to city streets, hills and gravel rides. Its dual 1,000W brushless motors deliver up to 2,688W of peak power, giving riders the extra muscle to accelerate confidently, climb steep neighborhood hills and keep moving when the pavement ends. A nearly 1 kWh battery provides up to 90 km (~56 miles) of range, making longer commutes and multiple stops around town easier to manage between charges. The 10×3″ puncture-resistant tubeless tires help maintain traction while reducing the risk of flats, and an adjustable dual swingarm suspension smooths out potholes, cracked pavement and rough gravel. With a top speed of 38 mph and the ability to tackle grades up to 34%, the L2 Max has plenty of performance in reserve for hard commutes and demanding rides, while its front and rear disc brakes with E-ABS help bring that power under control when traffic (or wildlife) demands a quick stop.

Regularly priced at $1,049, the L2 Max Dual Motor is on sale this month for $809, and $799 for Electrek readers.

Built for riders who refuse to choose between range and performance, the DT2 Pro packs dual 1,100W motors producing more than 2,900W of peak power. That’s enough muscle to tackle steep hills and grades of up to 36%, even when the route gets challenging, while its nearly 40 mph top speed gives riders plenty of acceleration for open stretches. The DT2’s 1.22 kWh battery delivers up to 115 km (~71 miles) of claimed range, making it a strong option for longer commutes or riders who want to cover several trips without stopping to recharge. Its 10×3″ puncture-resistant tires provide a wider contact patch for added traction, while an adjustable suspension front and rear helps absorb bumps, cracks, and rough patches to keep the rider stable and comfortable across changing terrain.

Regularly priced at $1,349, the DT2 Pro is on sale this month for $1,069, and $1,059 for Electrek readers.

In a recent development, taking the Gosoul 2 to the next level, the Gosoul 2 Pro Dual Motor packs a pair of 1,400W motors for a 36 mph top speed and the ability to tackle grades of up to 33%. An 864 Wh battery provides up to 90 km (~56 miles) of range, while the Ausom ShocFree dual swingarm suspension and 10×2.75″ tubeless tires help keep things smooth and stable on all kinds of roads and paths.

Regularly priced at $999, the Gosoul 2 Pro Dual Motor is on sale for $829, and $799 for Electrek readers.

The K20 Pro Dual Motor packs plenty of performance into a more approachable package, with dual 1,400W motors delivering 2,800W of peak power – more than enough to give riders the go-power they need to carve up modern day traffic and tackle grades of up to 33%, while its 36 mph top speed leaves plenty of headroom for open stretches. Its 864 Wh battery provides up to 90 km (~56 miles) of claimed range, making it a practical option for hard commutes or a full day of riding around town. ShocFree suspension and 10×2.75″ tubeless tires help smooth out potholes, uneven pavement and light off-road sections, while front and rear disc brakes with E-ABS provide maximum control during emergency stops.

Regularly priced at $879, the K20 Pro Dual Motor is on sale for just $689, and Electrek readers can do even better at $679.

Recent findings suggest that just like it says on the tin, the F1 Max offers maximum performance inspired by the pinnacle of motorsport. Built for riders who want their electric scooter to be considerably more than a commuter, this one delivers up to 3,840W of peak power, pushing the F1 Max to speeds of up to 45 mph and allowing it to tackle grades as steep as 38%. A 1.25 kWh battery pack gives riders 100 km (~62 miles) of range, while an adjustable dual-swingarm suspension and 10×3″ tubeless tires give the scooter the hardware to handle everything from broken city pavement and gravel to light off-road trails. Hydraulic disc brakes with E-ABS help bring all that performance back under control, while a 330 lb. maximum load and wide deck make the F1 Max a substantial machine for bigger, bolder riders ready for longer trips into the wilderness and anyone looking for a little LOT more excitement from their electric scooter.

Regularly priced at $1,549, the Ausom F1 Max is available at the awesome price of just $1,429 for Electrek readers with code ElectrekFB.

Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine.
  • Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is crucial since the body cannot make them.
  • Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine. Participants took either a daily high dose supplement of omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or a placebo.Fish oil is one of the most familiar ways people get omega-3s. However, the supplement in this clinical trial wasn’t made from fish, Hussein Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health with Keck Medicine of USC and the study’s lead researcher, told Healthline. This article uses the broader term omega-3 supplements.The researchers found that taking supplements raised omega-3 levels in participants’ brains, yet it didn’t change their memory, thinking skills, or brain structure.Dung Trinh, MD, an internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings challenge the common belief that omega-3 supplements, such as fish oil, can help prevent Alzheimer’s disease or improve memory.Millions of older adults take omega-3 supplements. In a 2017–2018 federal survey, 21.8% of U.S. adults age 60 and older reported taking an omega-3 fatty acid supplement in the past 30 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is crucial since the body cannot make them.

Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.

Subjects obtained little DHA from their diets and had at least one risk factor for dementia. Of the 365 people who enrolled, 225 completed the trial, according to the study. Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4.Participants took either 2,000 milligrams (mg) of DHA or a placebo every day. Neither participants nor researchers knew who received the supplement.

The supplement in the trial contained more than 90% DHA and about 1% EPA, Yassine stated.

Researchers found that high dose omega-3 supplements raised DHA levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord by 17%.

According to recent reports, both groups in the trial scored about the same on memory and thinking tests. Brain structure appeared the same in both groups.

It has been revealed that the supplement also raised omega-3 levels in the blood. Over two years, participants’ omega-3 index, a measure of EPA and DHA in red blood cells, rose from 4.9% to 11%.“That’s a massive increase, but that doesn’t translate into clinical outcomes,” Yassine stated.DHA reached the brain equally well in people with and without the gene variant APOE4, which is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, according to the study.Earlier trials couldn’t tell whether DHA failed to reach the brain or reached it without helping, the study’s authors say. This trial answers that open question, since the DHA got there.“This tells us that just because a supplement reaches the brain doesn’t necessarily mean it will improve brain function or prevent cognitive decline,” Trinh said.

According to recent reports, the lack of measurable change in memory and thinking may come down to how the body uses omega-3s, according to Yassine.He said it’s “really important to distinguish between omega-3 metabolism and omega-3 supplements.”A supplement can raise omega-3 levels, yet the body may still break them down before they reach the right places. Obesity, smoking, and a lack of exercise can all reduce how much omega-3 gets into the brain, he said.

According to recent reports, some fish and fish oil supplements may offer more than omega-3s. These sources may also include other nutrients such as lutein, vitamin E, and selenium, Yassine remarked.A supplement can raise the level, but if you don’t change the holistic program, just going and increasing the level by itself may not be sufficient,” he said.Researchers tend to fall into two camps on how to read the results, according to Yassine.

Some see the findings as evidence that supplements don’t work in isolation. Others argue the trial would need a longer follow-up or sicker participants to answer the question.Trinh pointed to the study’s length. “It’s also crucial to recognize that Alzheimer’s disease develops over decades, so a two-year study may not be long enough to determine whether DHA supplementation has any long-term preventive benefits,” he noted.

Fish oil supplements contain two omega-3 fatty acids, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Foods such as fish and flaxseed also contain omega-3s, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS).Research suggests omega-3s may help reduce inflammation, support heart health, and promote childhood growth and development.

Some observational studies link diets high in omega-3s with a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

Recent findings suggest that researchers say omega-3s may help preserve cognition by supporting brain cells in continuing to function and maintain their membranes, according to the ODS.“Omega-3s are important for the brain, and we and many others have shown that having higher levels of omega-3s is associated with less Alzheimer’s pathology, better cognition, and many other protective outcomes,” Yassine said, in contrast to the trial findings.Trinh agreed. “DHA plays an essential role in maintaining healthy brain cells, and there is evidence that eating fish as part of a healthy dietary pattern may support long-term brain health,” he said.Research on omega-3s and brain health is ongoing, and there is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness.

Some people may still benefit from a supplement, according to Yassine, including:.

Some neurologists test omega-3 levels, though the test isn’t standard, Yassine said.People with nutritional deficiencies or certain genetic or metabolic traits may respond differently to omega-3 supplements, and researchers still need to learn who might benefit, Trinh said.

People who already take fish oil or other omega-3 supplements for other reasons, such as high triglycerides, should make those decisions with their healthcare professionals, he stated.

Trinh stated he tells his patients that “what is good for the heart is generally good for the brain.” He recommended the following healthy habits:.

“Overall, this study reminds us that there is no magic pill for preventing Alzheimer’s disease and that maintaining brain health requires a much broader approach,” Trinh noted.

How much trash is on the moon? About 412,000 pounds.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that since the Soviet Union’s Luna 2 probe crashed into the moon’s surface in 1959, the first-ever human-made object to reach the moon, humanity has racked up over 140 missions to our only natural satellite.
  • Sources indicate that but these leftovers aren’t all space junk.
  • A significant chunk of the space trash on the moon consists of old landing gear from previous moon visits, Aidan Cowley, a science officer at the European Space Agency, tells Popular Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that since the Soviet Union’s Luna 2 probe crashed into the moon’s surface in 1959, the first-ever human-made object to reach the moon, humanity has racked up over 140 missions to our only natural satellite. These missions have delivered 12 humans, seven lunar rovers, and 412,000 pounds (187,000 kilograms) of discarded materials to the moon’s surface. That’s the weight of a Boeing 747 passenger plane.

Sources indicate that but these leftovers aren’t all space junk. In fact, some of this debris may prove useful for future lunar exploration.

A significant chunk of the space trash on the moon consists of old landing gear from previous moon visits, Aidan Cowley, a science officer at the European Space Agency, tells Popular Science.

Recent findings suggest that early moon exploration missions, like NASA’s Apollo missions, would land on the moon using a non-reusable lunar module, claims Cowley. “It would land, and then the top part of that module would return back to lunar orbit to rendezvous with the command module and return back to Earth. So, the base part of this vehicle would remain.”.

Leftover lunar rovers—manned or unmanned land vehicles used to explore the moon’s surface—also contribute to the growing mass of junk. These include China’s robotic Yutu rover, which sent information back to Earth for 31 months, as well as those that crash-landed, like the United Arab Emirates’s Rashid rover.

Industry observers note that other trash on the moon includes scientific equipment, toolboxes, and lunar impactor probes. These are devices that smash into the moon’s surface, not by accident, but to fulfill specific objectives, like close-up imaging or to fire rocks and dust into the air for analysis.

Recent findings suggest that images of the moon’s barren landscape might make you think that these lunar leftovers simply sit around undisturbed until the visit of the next crewed mission. But that’s not the case.

The moon is an incredibly harsh environment. It’s “constantly bombarded with micrometeorites,” explains Cowley. These tiny rock chunks, along with intense radiation, sunlight exposure, and dramatic temperature swings, will steadily wear down and damage objects.

The iconic American flag planted on the moon by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin in 1969, for example, has likely been bleached almost white by the sun.

But some of this damaged, degraded material could still have value for future moon exploration. Cowley claims samples of human equipment on the moon could be assessed to understand how the environment alters them.

Studying the impact of micrometeorites on equipment, for example, “might allow us to produce better solar cell or solar panel protection, so they don’t get degraded for humans when humans may eventually live on the moon,” claims Cowley.

In 1960, scientists predicted the world would end on November 13, 2026.

Why can’t we just launch all of Earth’s garbage into the sun?

What happens to your body when you die in space?

What would happen if Yellowstone’s ‘supervolcano’ erupted today?

Is turbulence really like Jell-O? Pilots weigh in.

Ahead of plans by NASA and the China National Space Agency to send crewed missions to the moon in the next five years, more equipment will likely amass on the lunar surface. But there are reasons to think these future missions may leave less of a mess behind.

“You might see more emphasis these days on vehicles that have a reusable aspect,” indicates Cowley. “Maybe the lander can land as one unit and take off as one unit again,” he says. Spaceships in development like SpaceX’s Starship Human Landing System (HLS) plan to adopt this reusable design.

Even if more equipment doesn’t accumulate on the moon, Cowley says the ESA has made plans to reuse some of this moon trash. One project has explored the potential of 3D printing methods to incorporate lunar scrap into new materials. Such efforts will have to account for the likelihood that such materials will be contaminated by lunar dust—sharp, shard-like particles of the rocky lunar surface that can prove a further hazard to machinery.

Cowley says that the lightweight aluminum that makes up the shell of many lunar vehicles could be melted down using concentrated sunlight.

“Rather than bringing things here with you or mining them on the moon,” claims Cowley, “you could actually just reuse the old equipment in the same way we recycle stuff down here on Earth.”.

That lunar “junk” may prove invaluable to the first humans to one day call the moon home. Or, as the old saying goes, one person’s trash is another person’s treasure.

#75428. Tesla Cybercab has crashed 8 times, and the data reveals a speed problem

Tesla Cybercab has crashed 8 times, and the data reveals a speed problem

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1161 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.
  • Recent findings suggest that four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph.
  • The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.

Recent findings suggest that four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph. The other four happened with a test driver on board and Tesla’s driver-assist engaged, including one where a Cybercab hit a car at 53 mph on a highway in Philadelphia.

The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.

Tesla files Cybercab crashes under NHTSA’s Standing General Order in two separate datasets.

The first is the ADS (Automated Driving System) file, which covers Level 4 driverless operation. That’s the Robotaxi service, where nobody is in the driver’s seat. NHTSA’s latest ADS release, published this month, contains 43 unique Tesla reports, up from 22 in July. Four are Cybercabs:.

Recent findings suggest that those are minor. Two weren’t Tesla’s fault at all, and none involved an injury.

According to recent reports, the second bucket is the Level 2 ADAS file, which covers driver-assist systems like Autopilot and “Full Self-Driving” (Supervised). Tesla has been testing Cybercabs fitted with steering wheels and a human behind them, often in places where it has no Robotaxi permit. Those crashes land in the ADAS file, with the driver type coded “In-Vehicle (Commercial / Test)” and the system “Verified Engaged.”.

There are four of them, all in September 2026:.

Tesla redacted the narrative of all four as confidential business information, so there’s no way to tell from the public data who was at fault or what the system was doing. Pennsylvania State Police, Austin Police, Lehi Police, and Florida Highway Patrol are listed as the investigating agencies.

The Philadelphia crash is not the Broad Street crash where a Cybercab lost its door panel that we reported in October. That one happened on a city street in October. This one happened on a highway in September, at around 10 p.m. local time.

Tesla has no permit to run automated vehicles in Pennsylvania, and it doesn’t run Robotaxi in Utah either. In Utah, a Cybercab was photographed in Park City in September with a driver visible behind the wheel.

Two of the eight Cybercab crashes involved injuries. Both are in the Level 2 file.

Across all 43 Tesla Robotaxi reports in the ADS file, the highest pre-crash speed is 29 mph. That was a driverless Model Y with two riders hitting a pothole in Dallas in September, after which one rider said they sought medical care. The median speed across all 43 reports is 1 mph.

Recent findings suggest that not one of those 43 crashes happened on a highway. Tesla coded 21 on streets, 15 in parking lots, and 7 at intersections.

Those numbers say more about where Tesla lets the system drive than about the software itself. As we reported last month, Robotaxi sticks to low-speed routes inside small geofenced zones and largely stays off highways.

The Robotaxi Safety Report Tesla published on October 21 claims zero people injured by Robotaxi over 3,112,541 driverless miles between January 22 and October 18. It doesn’t mention the Cybercab’s test fleet, and it excludes every mile driven with a safety monitor on board.

Take the speed cap off and the picture changes.

Recent findings suggest that in the Level 2 data, Teslas with Autopilot or FSD engaged regularly crash at highway speeds. Our master dataset of Tesla’s ADAS reports holds 69 fatal crashes. Among the 52 where Tesla recorded a speed, the median was 53 mph, the same speed the Cybercab was going in Philadelphia, and 29 happened at 50 mph or more.

Today alone, we matched three fatal crashes to Tesla’s latest filings:.

Engagement within 30 seconds of a crash, which is what triggers these reports, doesn’t prove the system caused it. But the pattern is consistent. At low speeds in a tight geofence, Tesla’s crashes are scrapes with chains, curbs, and potholes. At highway speeds, they can kill.

The Cybercab test fleet is where those two worlds overlap. It’s the same vehicle Tesla runs driverless in Austin, and the one Cybercab crash on record at real speed happened at 53 mph on a Philadelphia highway.

The Cybercab’s four driverless crashes are minor, and some weren’t Tesla’s fault. No one is denying that. But minor crashes still count, and so do the four Level 2 crashes that Tesla’s “zero injuries” framing leaves out. Both datasets describe the same vehicle running Tesla’s self-driving software.

It's looked to me for a while now that many of the improvements that people feel when they use FSD is not just the system getting better, but Elon pulling off the guardrails so the system attempts to do more stuff.

What the data shows is that Tesla has a speed problem. Its Robotaxi service looks clean largely because Tesla keeps it slow, off highways, and inside small zones. That’s also what makes it far less useful than a real ride-hailing service. You can’t take a Cybercab to the airport if the airport is on the other side of a freeway.

It has been revealed that to be clear, we think Tesla is right to do it this way. Given what the Level 2 data shows at 50+ mph, letting driverless Cybercabs onto highways today would be reckless.

It has been revealed that but it means the hard part is still ahead. Highways, larger geofences, and higher speeds are where crashes become fatal, and that’s where Tesla needs its system to be nearly perfect before it can scale. The Cybercab’s test crashes suggest it isn’t there yet. The question is how long Tesla can keep growing a robotaxi network that can’t go fast.

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • In chemistry, the concept of activation energy is the minimum amount of energy required to start a chemical reaction.
  • I can’t speak to this concept in chemistry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

In chemistry, the concept of activation energy is the minimum amount of energy required to start a chemical reaction. Metaphorically, this concept can be applied to psychology, thinking about both formal behavioral activation and initiating typical life tasks. I (JS) have often felt like there is an activation energy for everyday things we need to do. How much energy would it take to get myself to start cleaning the bathroom or to start exercising or to make dinner when I feel like just having a bowl of cereal? How much energy would it take for our clients to start doing the things we talk about them doing in session? What would it take for them to get out of bed, practice a new coping strategy, or talk with their partner or children in a more effective way? Sometimes it just feels impossible to get started, like there’s a barrier to overcome.

I can’t speak to this concept in chemistry. It has been many years since I was in a chem lab. However, when difficulty following through comes up in psychotherapy, I have some ideas that relate to the concept of activation energy. And this comes up a lot. Very simply, we can either lower barriers, therefore reducing the metaphorical activation energy necessary, or increase the energy we have to initiate the intended activity or task.

Recent findings suggest that to increase the energy you have, you might look at what gives you start-up energy (to activate), what drains you, and maybe what sustains your energy. Your schedule might be too full or just inefficient. There might be ways to rejigger things so that you have larger chunks of open time. Perhaps doing something that gets you excited and recharged can help propel you into doing something challenging. Maybe even playing energetic music while getting ready and doing the task. Planning to reward yourself after starting or completing the task may help you get excited—“eyes on the prize” and all that. Whatever strategy you come up with should be individualized to what works for you, what is doable, and what will help with follow-through.

Recent findings suggest that then there is the idea of decreasing the activation energy to start a task. What will make it easier to start or complete a task? Again, this will be individualized to both the task and the person, but here are some examples:.

The basic question is how do we get the chemical reaction, or the behavior, started. There is not a uniform answer, but there is a useful concept to apply. What will lower the activation energy required to get the job started? You might find that using the concept of activation energy provides a framework for successful task initiation. And, according to Mary Poppins, “Well begun is half done" (Stevenson, 1964, 0:28:15).
