Eagles are eating human-sized baboons in the Sahara desert

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (562 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An isolated  group of primates calls the rugged, sandstone Ennedi plateau in northern Chad, home.
  • New research published today in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology details how these eagles appear to be preying upon these nearly human-sized baboons.
  • Our ancestors were vulnerable to several predators, including crocodiles, big cats, and even eagles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An isolated  group of primates calls the rugged, sandstone Ennedi plateau in northern Chad, home. In this region in the middle of the Sahara Desert about the size of Switzerland, the olive baboons (Papio anubis) have lived a separate life away from other primate species. At 40 to 60 pounds, some olive baboons are about the size of our early hominin ancestors. But their size does not keep them safe from hungry Verreaux’s eagles (Aquila verreauxii).

New research published today in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology details how these eagles appear to be preying upon these nearly human-sized baboons. The discovery is reshaping how scientists think about predator-prey interactions during human evolution.

Our ancestors were vulnerable to several predators, including crocodiles, big cats, and even eagles. However, scientists believed that our species (Homo sapiens) and our hominin ancestors have been escaping these predators for roughly the past 2.5 million years. No primate over 28.6 pounds (13 kilograms) has been confirmed to be killed by raptors, so our body sizes appeared to be too heavy for even the large eagles with a 71- to 86-inch-long wingspan to pick up.

Industry observers note that in this study, the team describes skulls and bones of adult male olive baboons that bear the signature marks of eagle predation. There were talon punctures to the skulls, and various scrapes and “rakes” on the shoulder bones.

“We saw the eagles while we were searching for the baboons, but we never imagined that they might be a threat to them,” Catherine Hobaiter, a study co-author and primatologist at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, said in a statement. “Then we found the first skull with a puncture mark, and then another, and another.”.

With these remains, the team was able to calculate how much the deceased baboons weighed. One individual was over 57.3 pounds (26 kilograms), well within the range of a hominin species.

Sources indicate that “Having worked in this region for about three years, I had the opportunity to visit these gueltas (pockets of water that form within rock formations) and often observed Verreaux’s eagles. I had never imagined that these predators would target primates of this size until the research team stumbled upon evidence,” added Dr. Jean Didier Akpona from the African Parks Network. “This discovery leads us to explore further the mystery that surrounds the gueltas of the Sahara Desert.”.

To defend against eagles, our primate ancestors would “mob” or charge the attacker to try to drive them away. The modern primates living in places with eagle predators often move in large groups mixed with other primate species. This also mirrors the evolutionary history of our early ancestors, who lived alongside other hominin species and other primates. While some conflict arose, plenty of cooperative advantages to sticking together also happened—like mobbing eagles.

The team hopes to learn more about the lives of the Ennedi baboons to see what other evolutionary secrets they may be holding.

“Baboons are some of the best studied monkeys in Africa, but our very first observations from Ennedi upended all sorts of notions about what these baboons should be doing—from their diet to their social lives, I can’t wait to see what new ‘rules’ they’ll break next!” Hobaiter concluded.

#75353. The Gift of Gratitude

The Gift of Gratitude

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1445 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • Certain times of the year or milestone moments can increase the frequency with which we turn to appreciating the good, though this practice actually has value every single day of the year.
  • It has been revealed that the positive psychology movement has helped individuals focus more on what is strong rather than only on what is wrong.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

Certain times of the year or milestone moments can increase the frequency with which we turn to appreciating the good, though this practice actually has value every single day of the year.

It has been revealed that the positive psychology movement has helped individuals focus more on what is strong rather than only on what is wrong. As a therapist who works with individuals at various life stages and in situations of distress, I know and embrace the fact that we can’t ignore the overwhelming symptoms, heartache, trauma, and pain; however, I also believe that every individual has strengths and reserves of resilience that deserve to be incorporated and highlighted.

Some people find this practice of being thankful and looking for gratitude moments to be relatively easy, but others find this much more difficult and unnatural.

Several tips are offered here for consideration to build the gratitude muscle.

According to recent reports, like the recent movement to incorporate more bloom-scrolling rather than just doom-scrolling on our phones, the notion of being on the lookout for more positivity can turn out to be a welcome shift for many. We know the gloom and doom exist, and we have plenty of opportunities to focus on it, but also actively seeking out more of the positive, the good, and the upbeat can be incredibly beneficial. Rather than dismissing the negative news or ignoring the overwhelming, we are making room for balance in our bodies and brains.

We can be in charge of our media meal initiative and how we choose to budget our time and attention.

The idea of being on the lookout for gratitude moments is sometimes mistaken for waiting for those “big-ticket” items in life, like a windfall of money, a long-awaited vacation, or a promotion at work. While momentous moments are terrific, they tend to be rarer. However, the small moments of appreciating a delicious meal, a story about an everyday hero, a more scenic route home, the feel of a favorite blanket, or a beautiful bird on a branch are available to us on a much more regular basis.

There is a Japanese concept of Ma, which translates to the gap, interval, or space between things. This is often referenced in Japanese architecture, art, or conversation, but the notion of embracing space or pause can also be utilized in this pursuit of the positive. The gap or interval is not empty or useless; instead, it represents a meaningful void full of potential. So even in those moments between hearing difficult news, awaiting dreaded test results, or anticipating the next migraine headache, we can attempt to orient to something small, quiet, amusing, or pleasant for which we can feel grateful.

We can absolutely embrace the big, but we might as well also be on the lookout for the small because they are much more plentiful, readily available, and repeatable.

Being aware of possible triggers in our environment can have value and usefulness, but orienting toward noticing the glimmers internally and externally is often underutilized.

Glimmers are those small moments of calm or joy that can cue safety and relaxation for the nervous system. The notion of looking for glimmers was introduced by Deb Dana and based on work by Stephen Porges1, and this practice cues the body toward a state of safety and grounding rather than the fight-flight-freeze mode of response that is activated under threat.

Even on really bad days (or maybe even especially on really bad days), we can choose to notice some good or gratifying things.

Glimmers are the opposite of triggers; both exist in our world, and we deserve to be able to know how to be alert to both.

According to recent reports, when we are actively looking for more positive, joyful, beautiful, interesting, or unique in our daily world, we begin to see more of it. Sometimes that elegant, sturdy tree, beautifully colored house, smell of our favorite beverage, or sparkling ray of sunlight coming through the window at a certain time of day has gone unnoticed until we take the time to notice. And once we notice, we tend to orient to seeing it again and again—along with that more satisfying sense of appreciation on repeat.

Recent findings suggest that orienting to some good news, a funny joke, the stuffy nose that finally cleared up, an enthusiastic pet greeting, or a beloved song on the playlist can all be wonderful in the moment, but what really allows the biggest benefit is to allow the positivity to fully soak in. Like attending to a spill on the counter, dipping a sponge into the corner of the spill for just a moment won’t be as effective as slowly, carefully moving the sponge around the spill to fully absorb the liquid.

When we pause to fully notice the benefits, orient the multi-sensorial delights, and stay with it for several moments, we are more wholeheartedly allowing the affirmative and encouraging to register in our systems. And if we choose to later repeat this positive moment in a journal or in a recounting to someone else, the benefits multiply and the positivity is reinforced.

Intentionally, mindfully staying aware of the positive is a happiness hack. And savoring the moment can be a superpower.

Various research studies support the notion that optimistic, grateful people are happier, calmer, more empathetic, less stressed, have better physical health, and even live longer2. Neuroimaging results (MRI and fMRI) also show that practicing gratitude engages key brain regions involved in reward processing and emotional regulation3. These findings support the incredible connection between mind and body.

Industry observers note that studied gratitude interventions include gratitude journals, gratitude letters or texts, and other methods of counting more blessings than burdens. Although there are various self-administered psychological interventions that can improve overall well-being (such as spending time in nature, mindfulness, or acts of kindness), psychological science does consistently show that gratitude practices improve overall mental and physical health.

In a recent development, even if this skill of looking for gratitude, positivity, and thankfulness doesn’t come easily or naturally to you, strive to refrain from self-blame about this. People have a wide variety of circumstances that can influence their ability to orient toward the good, and some of this is influenced by such things as external life circumstances and even genetics. The negativity bias in human brains is also well established and did have an evolutionary benefit4, but times are different now. A broader, more balanced perspective can help. And because brains are neuroplastic, practice in these skills makes for more permanence with these skills.

Be on the lookout for the lovely, and you, too, can optimize your inner optimist.

Low-Calorie Diet and Supervised Exercise May Reverse Early Onset Type 2 Diabetes

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The RESET for Remission trial, presented at the 2026 European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas on October 1, found that more than half of adults with early onset type 2 diabetes entered remission after six months on a low calorie diet and supervised exercise program.
  • Early onset type 2 diabetes is when the condition is diagnosed before age 45.
  • Those with early onset type 2 diabetes may be at a higher risk of complications like long-term damage to the capillaries (microvascular complications), adverse cardiovascular outcomes, and earlier death.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The RESET for Remission trial, presented at the 2026 European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas on October 1, found that more than half of adults with early onset type 2 diabetes entered remission after six months on a low calorie diet and supervised exercise program.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is when the condition is diagnosed before age 45.

Those with early onset type 2 diabetes may be at a higher risk of complications like long-term damage to the capillaries (microvascular complications), adverse cardiovascular outcomes, and earlier death.

Typical treatment for early onset type 2 diabetes is often a combination of lifestyle changes, like diet and exercise, and medications.

However, this new study suggests that a supervised low calorie diet and exercise program may help some people with early onset type 2 diabetes enter remission.

The RESET for Remission trial included 96 adults from England and Canada who were between the ages of 18 and 45, had early onset type 2 diabetes, obesity, and were not on insulin treatment.

The participants had an average age of 38 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 35.2 kg/m2. They were randomized into a control group that received usual care alone and the intervention group, which ate a low calorie diet and participated in supervised exercise programs.

During the first 12 weeks, participants in the intervention group followed an 800–900-calorie-per-day diet and completed twice-weekly supervised aerobic and resistance exercise sessions, along with one independent exercise session per week.

For weeks 13–24, they transitioned to a weight-maintenance diet and independent exercise.

Both groups were supervised by physicians, and the intervention group was also closely supervised by licensed dietitians.

The low calorie diet consisted of 30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, and 20% fat. Participants were also encouraged to drink at least 2 liters of calorie-free fluids per day and given access to a fiber-based laxative as needed.

In the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). Then, in weeks 3–12, the participants maintained the same calorie intake but had more flexibility in their food choices.

It has been revealed that this second phase of the diet included one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables. Typically, this meant 60 to 90 grams of protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, and two portions of non-starchy vegetables.

Sources indicate that at the end of 24 weeks, 54% of the intervention group entered remission of type 2 diabetes, compared with only 4% in the control group. Researchers defined remission as an HbA1c level below 6.5% without glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks.

“This study proves what most physicians have advocated for quite some time. Clearly, diet and exercise can work to improve or even resolve diabetes,” David Cutler, MD, board certified family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline.

It has been revealed that cutler also added that this study provides a clear example of how difficult it can be to enter diabetes remission with diet and exercise alone. He stated that the small number of participants in the study also makes him wonder if these findings can be applied to all populations.

Another limitation of this study, as Cutler pointed out, was that the strict dietary limits imposed on study participants would be very difficult for the average adult to adhere to.

The study also followed participants for only six months, so it’s unclear how many would remain in remission over the longer term.

“It is worth trying diet and exercise first because they can work to achieve meaningful weight loss and remission of diabetes,” he said.

It may be possible to prevent or delay the onset of type 2 diabetes by:.

The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) notes that losing 5%–7% of your body weight can help reduce your risk of type 2 diabetes.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is a growing concern worldwide, coinciding with the rise of obesity.

Research from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) projects that the number of people in the United States under age 20 with type 2 diabetes could reach 220,000 by 2060. This is an increase of 700%.

Sources indicate that people diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at a younger age face more decades of living with the condition, along with a higher risk of developing complications earlier in life and reduced life expectancy. These complications can develop as early as midlife and include:.

Speak with a healthcare professional about your risk of type 2 diabetes and changes you might be able to make in order to prevent or delay diagnosis.

A later diagnosis can help reduce the risk of some complications of the condition.

Before public bathrooms, women were kept on a ‘urinary leash.’ Then department stores changed everything.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, what’s the weirdest thing you learned this week?
  • Recent findings suggest that today’s episode features the three hosts of Vanity Veritas, a delightful podcast about the history of beauty.
  • For most of modern human history, a woman’s range of motion in the world was limited by how long she could hold her pee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, what’s the weirdest thing you learned this week? Well, whatever it is, we promise you’ll have an even weirder answer if you listen to PopSci’s hit podcast. The Weirdest Thing I Learned This Week hits Spotify, YouTube, Apple, and everywhere else you listen to podcasts every-other Wednesday morning. It’s your newly introduced favorite source for the strangest science-adjacent facts, figures, and Wikipedia spirals the editors of Popular Science can muster. If you like the stories in this post, we guarantee you’ll love the show.

Recent findings suggest that today’s episode features the three hosts of Vanity Veritas, a delightful podcast about the history of beauty. VV’s co-host Kristina dove into the history of public toilets—and the longstanding lack thereof, at least for women.

For most of modern human history, a woman’s range of motion in the world was limited by how long she could hold her pee. Historians call this the “urinary leash.”.

You might be wondering how this could possibly be a gendered problem, given the universality of the need to urinate. There was almost certainly a time when humans of all types could duck behind trees (or not) and relieve themselves with pretty similar levels of comfort and ease. But by the time Ancient Romans were using public latrines in the 2nd century BC, women of good standing weren’t supposed to go anywhere near them.

According to recent reports, so when “monkey closets”—the first public flush toilets—debuted at London’s Great Exhibition in 1851, women didn’t benefit much. Some men thought women would be (or maybe should be) too embarrassed to enter a public restroom, so they were often excluded. And sometimes, if bathrooms were installed for women, they were sabotaged by men who took offense. By the time municipal toilets started popping up, they were often isolated and unsupervised, which meant even women willing to break the taboo had to worry about safety concerns. A woman on the go might come across a genteel lounge reserved for ladies, but they were designed for swooning in and kept decidedly toilet-free.

Ergo the “urinary leash”: you could only travel as far as your bladder allowed. That’s about two to five hours, if you don’t want to put your health at risk. Keep in mind that this was before cars, so a trip across the city would easily take up a good chunk of that time.

The options when you were away from home were pretty grim. You could take a wide-stance squat over a grate, if you were desperate. On the one hand, bloomer crotches were split down the middle to allow for easy evacuation. On the other hand, a woman would have four to eight layers of skirts to try to protect from backsplash. Wealthy ladies might use a fancy porcelain urinal called a “bourdaloue.” (Fun fact: Many antique dealers now sell these as gravy boats.).

In a recent development, the solution? Department stores. Obviously the actual solution was just providing women with decent public bathrooms, but no one bothered to do so until the owner of Marshall Field’s in Chicago realized that safe, clean toilets would draw women to the store—and allow them to shop for longer. Their luxurious facilities opened in 1907, and not a moment too soon. They featured extra-wide stalls (for bustles, naturally) and a staffed nursery.

Harry Selfridge, who rose up in the ranks at Marshall Field’s before striking out on his own, later took the idea to London when he opened his eponymous department store there. But he actually upped the ante and added hot running water, telephones, writing desks, and more. (Editor’s note: Please bring back department store coworking spaces.) Marshall Field’s and Selfridge’s weren’t doing this for the sake of women’s lib; a safe place to pee meant women could spend more time out of the house, which meant spending more money. But these spaces did set a precedent that helped activists push for women’s restrooms in more places, and they also made it easier for suffragists to hang out and strategize. In 2023, Selfridge’s celebrated its place in the history of peeing in public with Exhibition, an artwork by Gray Wielebinski reflecting on the rich cultural significance of communal bathrooms—and the threats they still face today.

These days, access to public bathrooms is nowhere near as widespread as it should be. That’s especially true for trans people, who have been subjected to a wave of state laws attempting to restrict which restrooms they can use. As the history of public toilets—and the dreaded urinary leash—should remind us, a bathroom isn’t “just a bathroom,” and restrictions on their use have a chilling effect on autonomy.

For more on the massive cultural impact of department stores, check out Vanity Veritas.

In a recent development, because this week’s episode featured three special guests, I decided to keep my fact short. Cockney rhyming slang—a code that came out of East London in the 19th century—is not a subject I have a lot to say about, but it is something I want to make sure you know exists. Contrary to popular belief, there’s no strong evidence that this cheeky and cryptic lexicon arose to facilitate criminal acts. But whatever fueled its creation, it’s persisted in various subcultures to this day. The system works like this: pick a phrase that rhymes with the word you’re actually referring to, then drop the part that actually rhymes. Tricky? Yes. Whimsical? Very.

According to recent reports, if you’ve ever wondered why that fart sound you make with your lips is called a “raspberry,” you have Cockney Rhyming Slang to thank. Fart rhymes with raspberry tart, which then gets shortened to raspberry. Things get stranger when you move into double and triple rhyme territory. “Bottle and glass” meant arse, so “bottle” did too. Then “bottle” got rhymed with Aristotle, which got shortened to “Aris,” which got rhymed with plaster of Paris. Congratulations, “plaster” now means butt.

You can check out a full dictionary of Cockney rhyming slang—with folks weighing in to confirm words or mark them as made-up “Mockney”.

Opera diva Maria Callas famously shed her weight with the help of a tapeworm, just like loads of Victorian women did. Right? Well, not quite. In fact, the truth is probably even more disgusting.

Actual opera singer (and Rachel’s sister!) Chelsea Feltman did a deep dive on Callas for Vanity Veritas a while back, so she dove into the nitty gritty of the tapeworm myth for this week’s Weirdest Thing.

In a recent development, maria Callas really did drop a troubling amount of weight over the course of 18 months in the 1950s, and she really did have a beef tapeworm. But according to a 2022 review in Parasitologia, the idea that the tapeworm was her go-to weightloss hack is actually backwards. She most likely caught the tapeworm as the result of the high-protein, rare-meat diet she favored for weight loss. Sources disagree on whether Callas ever infected herself on purpose, but the fact remains that this parasite was not a diet hack: Even a five-meter beef tapeworm wouldn’t cause much weight loss, though it could definitely leave you vitamin-deficient. Some tapeworms can even form cysts in your brain.

It has been revealed that the idea of popping worm pills popped up in December 1912, when the Washington Post reported that a society woman in Peoria had paid for two suspicious capsules that her husband then analyzed. Inside, he said, he found tapeworm parts. The woman, the vendor, and the government agent were never named, which strongly suggests this story was probably at least kinda made up. The next day, the surgeon general said he’d never seen such a pill, and the Hygienic Laboratory’s director called it the wildest story he’d heard in a while. The legend kept growing anyway, with a bigger price tag in an Ohio paper in 1914 and a comic-strip “diet doctor” with wriggling capsules in 1927. It may even trace back to an 1899 Indiana medicine-show man arrested for giving patients artificial tapeworms to “pass” as proof his cure worked. Mostly, this seems to be a cultural meme that served to mock vain, silly women.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, this hasn’t stopped real people from trying to take advantage of this fake historical trend. In 2013, Iowa’s state medical director warned about a patient who’d swallowed a tapeworm they bought online.

(If you’re looking for the picture of the cheese-baited tapeworm-catching device, here you go.).

Recent findings suggest that in the early 20th century, about 100 American women died of cervical cancer every day. The only diagnostic test was a biopsy, and by the time women experienced symptoms it was usually too late for anyone to help them. The test that changed it all came from a Greek immigrant who never set out to find it.

George Papanicolaou moved to New York in 1913 and drifted through odd jobs, including playing violin in a restaurant and a stint as a famously bad carpet salesman. He finally landed a lab gig under Charles Stockard, a prominent eugenicist who wanted to understand human reproduction as a means of better controlling it (ugh). There, Papanicolaou found he could swab live guinea pigs for cervical cells instead of doing invasive biopsies. He wondered whether the method would work on humans.

It has been revealed that his wife Mary became (human) guinea pig number one. For 21 years, she gave a sample almost every day—roughly 7,600 pap smears—while also staining slides, recruiting friends, and later training the technicians who read results. George introduced her to people as “my wife and victim.”.

Industry observers note that in 1925 George spotted cancer cells in a hospital sample. He took that historic discovery to a 1928 conference sponsored by eugenicists, where he presented blurry slides to doctors who preferred the biopsy method over his smear concept. Things… didn’t go well.

Industry observers note that it took Stockard’s death, a fresh boss for George, a collaboration testing more than 3,000 women, and artist Hashime Murayama’s vivid cell illustrations to turn the test into a medical landmark. By the late 1950s, women were lining up around the block for pap smears, and US cervical cancer deaths fell by about 70 percent.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when the mid-engine C111 sports-car concept made its debut at the Frankfurt auto show in 1969, would-be buyers sent blank checks to Mercedes-Benz headquarters. Despite the fervent interest, however, the C111 never went into production, although a handful of prototypes were built over the years. Now Mercedes-Benz has confirmed that it will auction off one of those cars, making it (at long last) the first C111 to reach private hands. And would-be buyers who wish to take home the C111 will need to muster that same blank-check energy.

See all results for used Mercedes-Benz for sale near 63129.

The C111 was conceived as the modern-day successor to the W198 300SL Gullwing of the 1950s. The two-seat supercar featured a mid-mounted rotary engine, a fiberglass body, and gullwing doors. The following year, an evolved C111-II was unveiled at the 1970 Geneva auto show with a 345-hp 2.4-liter four-rotor engine. The 1973 global oil embargo and the costs to meet rising emissions standards caused the firm to shelve the blueprint for series production, although several more C111 prototypes were made, including a C111-II-D with a diesel engine in 1976 and a diesel-powered C111-III in 1978. A total of 17 cars were made; 13 still exist. Mercedes has kept them all, until now.

In a recent development, the car being sold is a C111-II built in August 1970. It’s fitted with a 2.4-liter rotary engine making 345 horsepower at 7700 rpm, a five-speed manual transmission, anti-lock brakes, twin fuel tanks, and a Becker Europa radio. Weighing 2734 pounds, the C111-II had a claimed top speed of 186 mph and a 0-to-60-mph time of 4.8 seconds. It was used as a test car, including at the Hockenheimring.

Like most of the C111s, this car is painted Weissherbst orange; the seats are upholstered in houndstooth fabric. The car sits on modern 8-x-15-inch alloy wheels; the original magnesium wheels from 1970 are included, but with the caveat that they “are now suitable only for display purposes.” The anti-lock brake system is not functional.

The car has been on display at the Mercedes-Benz Museum since 2006. It was sympathetically restored in 2024 in preparation for an appearance at Pebble Beach. The odometer indicates 24,766 km (15,389 miles).

The car is being auctioned by RM Sotheby’s this coming February in Paris. The proceeds of the sale will help fund the museum, including an initiative to digitize its contents, part of the “Mercedes-Benz Museum 2.0” project.

See all results for used Mercedes-Benz for sale near 63129.

To reassure the future buyer that the value of their C111 won’t be diluted by additional examples coming onto the market, Mercedes-Benz has committed to a 25-year moratorium on any future sales of the remaining cars. Mercedes-Benz collectors, call your bankers.

According to recent reports, police in Canada say they have busted an organized auto theft crime ring that was stealing cars from the Great White North and shipping them across the ocean to Africa. Authorities revealed a total of over 200 charges against 12 arrested individuals associated with the crime. In addition, officers recovered more than 90 vehicles worth a combined $4.5 million Canadian—$3.15 million in U.S. dollars.

Sources indicate that while the charges and announcement came on Monday, authorities have been putting this case together since March, when officers of the Peel Regional Police in Ontario put together what they called “Project Cadetta” in partnership with the Canada Border Services Agency. Together, they initially focused on a single warehouse in Brampton, which allegedly was the staging area for stolen cars that were destined for West Africa via Canadian shipping ports. As police investigated the space, they began linking individuals to other locations.

Recent findings suggest that authorities say that many of these cars would get different VIN numbers as a part of the scheme. While they didn't detail the vehicles in question, they did show photos of a few; among them are several Lexus vehicles, a Land Rover Range Rover Sport, a Toyota Land Cruiser, and a BMW XM.

Sources indicate that if this sounds familar, it’s not just you; this year alone, we at Road & Track have reported on similar theft rings several times. In April, authorities in the U.S. charged six people with being part of an illegal operation to steal cars and ship them to Africa. Police linked the suspects to some 130 cars. Then, later in the same month, police in Newly introduced York said they found 72 more cars destined for West Africa. The cars in question included a Rolls-Royce, several BMWs, and an Audi SQ8. In May, Canadian police found another 40 stolen cars involved with a similar theft ring.

Why Being Home for the Holidays Makes You Feel 15 Again

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Industry observers note that every year, my clients tell me some version of the same story.
  • This topic frequently comes up in my sessions during the holiday season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Industry observers note that every year, my clients tell me some version of the same story. I've been making so much progress, but after five minutes at my parents' house, it all goes out the window.

This topic frequently comes up in my sessions during the holiday season. They've spent months learning to better manage their emotions, or set healthier boundaries, and they’re enjoying the benefits of that work in their day-to-day lives.

According to recent reports, then, when they go home for the holidays, they automatically fall back into old habits. They're arguing with their siblings like teenagers, getting defensive when their parents offer unsolicited advice, and agreeing to things they don't want to do just to keep the peace.

Does slipping back into familiar family dynamics mean you haven't actually changed? That underneath all that growth, you're still the same person you were at 17?

It has been revealed that long story short, the answer is “no.” Sliding into old roles is a completely normal, well-documented phenomenon in personality science. Let’s talk about why this happens—and what to do about it.

Personality traits are a descriptive summary of how you typically think and behave. Do you generally experience substantial emotions or are you less reactive? Do you usually strategy ahead or fly by the seat of your pants? Are you typically the person driving the conversation, or do you often find yourself hanging back to observe during social situations?

Importantly, personality is not black and white. Even though we often think about personality traits as categories (e.g., introvert vs. extrovert), traits actually exist on a continuum. People can fall anywhere along that spectrum (e.g., always introverted, often introverted, 50/50 depending on the situation, often extraverted, always extraverted).

Sources indicate that where you fall on a particular personality trait reflects how you tend to think, feel, and behave on average, across different situations. For example, you might be more extraverted when you're out with friends and much quieter in a work meeting.

You can shift that average, making it more likely that you'll think, feel, and behave in ways that align with your values. But even as your personality shifts, some situations will still bring out more or less of a particular trait. In other words, if you've become generally more confident and even-keeled in your everyday life, a few days of feeling insecure or emotionally reactive around your family doesn't mean you've lost the progress you've made.

And those personality averages do shift across our lives. Research demonstrates that, on average, people become more emotionally stable, more conscientious, and better able to get along with others as they age.

Much of this personality change takes place between ages 20 and 40, a period when many people leave their family homes and gain greater freedom to choose who they spend time with and how they spend their days.

Industry observers note that these new environments can encourage different patterns of behavior. Maybe growing up, you learned that raising your voice was the only way to get your point across. But in your adult friendships and romantic relationships, communicating calmly may be much more effective. As these healthier ways of interacting are reinforced over time, you may gradually become a more agreeable person.

Even if you've changed considerably over the years, your family may expect you to behave like your old self, and those expectations may pull you to fall back into old habits. For example, if you grew up trying to keep the peace by sacrificing your needs, you might find yourself agreeing to sleep in a separate room from your partner to appease your parents, even if you’ve been actively making progress toward being more assertive.

And the stress of the holidays doesn't help. When we're tired or otherwise stretched thin, we're more likely to fall back on well-practiced responses. The behaviors your family pulls from you were learned early and reinforced repeatedly, so under stress, your brain dusts them off because they require less energy than the newer patterns you might be working on.

Sources indicate that the good news is that being around your family gives you an opportunity to practice the new ways of thinking and behaving you’ve been working on. Think of it like playing a video game on hard mode: The skills are the same, but the challenges are tougher. You can't necessarily change how your family treats you, but you can make small changes in how you respond to them. And over time, those small changes can help create a different dynamic. Here are three ways to start:.

If you want to start showing up differently, The Personality Action Initiative helps you identify one specific action that could make the biggest difference in changing an old pattern and create a plan to put it into practice.

Latest Update: Mathematicians make a breakthrough in 174-year-old problem

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (693 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While mathematicians technically solved a nearly 175-year-old theorem known as the Four-Color Problem in 1976, the problem continues to vex researchers.
  • The underlying conceit to the Four-Color Problem is deceptively straightforward.
  • It took more than 85 years until a full proof arrived—a particularly notable moment, since it was also the first major theorem proven by a computer program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While mathematicians technically solved a nearly 175-year-old theorem known as the Four-Color Problem in 1976, the problem continues to vex researchers. For some in the field, their fascination with the perniciously complex concept runs so deep, that they liken their obsession to a lingering disease. But after a decade of analysis, an international team of mathematicians has made the first major breakthrough in the ongoing Four-Color Problem saga in 30 years. At this year’s Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS) conference, investigators laid out the optimal, most efficient algorithm that solves the Four-Color Problem.

The underlying conceit to the Four-Color Problem is deceptively straightforward. In 1852, 19th century English mathematician Francis Guthrie posited that you only need a quartet of hues to fill every border-enclosed region on a map. Think all territories, regions, states, and nations filled in with only four colors. The first proof was introduced in 1879, and seemed solid for 11 years. That is, until Guthrie’s colleagues found an error in the calculations.

It took more than 85 years until a full proof arrived—a particularly notable moment, since it was also the first major theorem proven by a computer program. However, many in the mathematical community took glitch with the digital discovery after having difficulty verifying it themselves.

A more accessible proof arrived in 1997, but even then, the algorithmic system became painfully slow as sample maps grew larger. A handful of mathematicians around the world have pondered new approaches to the problem ever since—including University of Copenhagen computer scientist Mikkel Thorup, who likens his interest to a “four-color disease.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I would guess that at least 1,000 mathematicians have caught the four-color disease, spending months trying to make it work but never quite succeeding,” Thorup noted in a university profile. “It is the disease people have suffered from since 1852.”.

It took years, but Thorup and his colleagues made progress after uncovering a novel detail regarding map-like surfaces known as planar graphs. The researchers realized these graphs feature many more reducible arrangements than experts previously assumed. This provided them a much more discreet set of starting points.

“Think of reducible configurations as handles you can grab hold on to start four-coloring,” added study co-author and Technical University of Denmark (DTU) mathematician Carsten Thomassen. “We show that graphs do not contain just one handle, but an astonishing number of them. Nobody knew that before.”.

Instead of one or two handles in a graph, the team could now identify many more handles throughout any given map. This allowed them to simultaneously begin filling regions with four colors, which exponentially quickened the overall process. Thomassen mentioned this boosted their algorithm from quadratic time (where calculation speed increases proportionally to the square of an input size) to linear time.

Sources indicate that “This means that if a map contains ten times as many regions, the computation only becomes about ten times slower. With the previous algorithm, it would have become about 100 times slower,” he added.

Industry observers note that but does this really change anything beyond theoretical mathematics? According to researchers, the answer is a resounding “yes.”.

“The remarkable thing is that because there are so many handles, the idea can also be applied to other kinds of surfaces besides a flat map,” stated Thorup. “For example, surfaces with holes, such as a swim ring or a piece of…cheese.”.

It has been revealed that okay, so the implications may be somewhat subtle for most people’s day-to-day lives. That doesn’t change the fact that mathematicians finally worked through symptoms of their disease for the first time in 30 years. As to why Thorup and his colleagues spent a decade on a theorem whose major immediate implications are “cheese,” he had a relatively succinct explanation.

“Because mathematicians are slightly crazy. Most of what mathematicians work on consists of very nerdy questions,” he said. “We become obsessed with this type of problem because it challenges the human intellect. And if we find the answer, we’ll probably also find answers to other mathematical puzzles.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A simple swap for salt could spare millions of cardiovascular disease-related deaths, upcoming research suggests.

In a study published in Nature Health on November 4, researchers at The George Institute for Global Health modeled the potential impact of 193 countries switching from regular table salt to potassium-enriched salt.

They found the switch could prevent nearly 3 million deaths and more than 10 million upcoming cases of heart and kidney disease worldwide each year.

In the United States, this simple salt swap could prevent nearly 105,000 deaths and about 492,000 fresh cases a year, the researchers estimated.

About 130.6 million U.S. adults have cardiovascular disease, according to the American Heart Association (AHA).

Liping Huang, PhD, a senior data analyst in the Food Policy Division at The George Institute for Global Health and co-lead author of the study, told Healthline the team started with current blood pressure levels by sex, age, and country.

The researchers then estimated how replacing all salt with a salt substitute would change people’s sodium and potassium intake, blood pressure, and disease risk, she noted.The team modeled a blend of 75% sodium chloride and 25% potassium chloride. The study estimated these yearly results worldwide:.

The authors wrote that the model relied on data from a few years ago and on many assumptions, and that any large-scale switch would take years.

Potassium-enriched salt replaces some of the sodium chloride in regular table salt with potassium chloride, according to The George Institute.Asked where other salts like kosher salt and sea salt fit in, Huang said those salts may contain some trace elements “which has those health halos around them, but essentially they’re still primarily sodium chloride.”Huang noted that potassium-enriched salt tastes “about the same as a regular table salt.” She said it’s possible a small number of people with a sensitive palate could taste a difference.

Huang said that “it’s really hard for people to cut back their salt intake.”“But the easier way is just to replace part of the sodium chloride in our normal salt with potassium chloride, because increasing potassium intake also helps to reduce blood pressure,” she said.The two minerals play opposite roles in the body, according to Cheng-Han Chen, MD, a board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“While sodium causes water retention and increased blood pressure, potassium will help the kidneys remove sodium from the body and lower blood pressure,” Chen told Healthline.Huang noted she worked on an earlier trial of about 21,000 people in 600 rural villages in northern China in 2021.

People who used potassium-enriched salt had a 14% lower risk of stroke, a 13% lower risk of cardiovascular events, and a 12% lower risk of early death than those who used regular salt, according to a 2021 study in The Latest England Journal of Medicine that summarized the trial’s results.

The World Health Organization (WHO) endorsed potassium-enriched salt in a 2025 guideline, saying it can reduce blood pressure and the risk of cardiovascular disease.

The AHA said potassium-based salt substitutes can help lower blood pressure in some adults. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued labeling guidance in 2020 allowing an alternate name for potassium chloride on ingredient labels to include the word “salt.”“We think that blood pressure begins to improve as soon as 1 week after cutting back on sodium intake. The full benefit typically takes up to 4 weeks,” Chen said.

“We generally recommend a daily sodium limit of 2,300 milligrams (mg), ideally under 1,500 mg a day. Most people consume over 3,000 mg of sodium a day, well above the recommended limit,” Chen noted.The WHO recommends less than 2,000 mg of sodium per day and suggests at least 3,510 mg of potassium a day.In the United States, more than 70% of salt intake comes from processed and restaurant foods, according to the AHA.

Huang said that some people with advanced chronic kidney disease should avoid potassium-enriched salt.When the kidneys don’t work well, the body may not clear extra potassium efficiently, she said. That can lead to hyperkalemia, or high potassium levels in the blood, which can raise the risk of cardiac arrest, Huang said.Among people with stage 3 to stage 5 kidney disease, switching to salt substitutes could prevent about 750,000 deaths a year by lowering blood pressure and cause about 100,000 deaths a year from hyperkalemia, the researchers estimated.The AHA said that people with kidney disease or who take medications that affect potassium should check with a healthcare professional before using these products.

An estimated 37 million U.S. adults have chronic kidney disease, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

In a recent development, potassium-enriched salt is available at supermarkets in the U.S. Many major U.S. grocery chains, including Kroger, Walmart, and Publix, carry two types of products, according to their websites:.

Potassium-enriched salt typically costs about twice as much as regular salt, according to the study.Huang stated she hoped people would see the results and start thinking of the switch as “a simple thing I can do for their own health.”.

BMW says the M3 EV will coexist with a gasoline-powered M3, which should arrive in showrooms ahead of the electric model.

BMW M vehicles have cultivated a devoted following for their sublime performance, and it stands to reason that BMW wouldn't risk tainting that legacy when the power comes from electrons instead of gasoline.

Expert Tip: If you can't wait for the M3 EV to launch before deciding on your next BMW sports sedan, consider the outgoing i4, which is one of our favorite EVs and can be had with a 592-hp dual-motor powertrain.

Recent findings suggest that everything. Details are scarce, but we know the M3 will ride atop BMW's new EV platform. Production is expected to begin sometime in 2027.

Car and Driver calculates your car's value in three free and easy steps - using the same Black Book® data dealers use to appraise vehicles.

The M3 EV will be powered by four electric motors producing a total of 838 horsepower and 885 pound-feet of torque. The motors themselves are of the electrically excited variety, and the quad-motor setup allows for torque vectoring both front to back and side to side. The car operates in rear-wheel-drive mode most of the time, with the front motors coming online when needed.

Recent findings suggest that the M3 EV utilizes BMW's "Heart of Joy" control unit and software, which handles the drivetrain, braking, charging, regeneration, and steering functions. When we drove a prototype of the electric M3, we found it to be a beast on the racetrack. We also experimented with the different drive modes, including the fake gearshifts and sounds in the various eDrive settings, but thought the car was best in Auto mode.

BMW says the electric M3 will come with a battery pack measuring roughly 100 kilowatt-hours. This should provide an EPA-rated driving range of around 300 miles, though we’re still awaiting official EPA estimates. DC fast-charging capability is remarked to be up to 420 kilowatts, which should enable the M3 to add a considerable amount of range in a short period of time.

Sources indicate that first Row: Like the i3, the M3 EV features BMW's latest digital dashboard, which features a trapezoidal infotainment display. The concept car pictured here shows deeply bucketed performance seats with five-point safety harnesses, but expect normal chairs and seatbelts on the production model. The concept vehicle also showed a cloth trim piece on the dashboard with multi-colored ambient backlighting.

Second Row: A pair of bucket seats was shown in the concept vehicle, although we think a three-across bench will at least be offered on the production M3 EV.

Cargo Capacity: We aren't sure about the M3 EV's cargo capacity yet, but we expect to see storage in both the trunk and the front trunk.

In a recent development, the touchscreen offers a high level of customization and features a matrix backlight for easy visibility in all conditions. BMW's latest Panoramic Vision system projects crucial information onto the lower part of the windshield, stretching from A-pillar to A-pillar. Logically, key driving information is displayed on the left for the driver, while central and right-hand areas of the display can be personalized and are visible to all occupants.

According to recent reports, up to six widgets can be moved from the infotainment screen to the Panoramic Vision system by drag and drop, and further customization of both screens can be manipulated by buttons on the steering wheel. A head-up display is available, and smartphones and smartwatches from all leading manufacturers can be programmed to operate as the vehicle key.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that henry Ford was racing cars before the Mustang, GT40, or even the Ford Motor Manufacturer itself existed. Back in 1901, he won his first race behind the wheel of a two-cylinder race car nicknamed “Sweepstakes,” a car that produced just 26 horsepower. 125 years later, Ford has unveiled the 815-horsepower 2028 Mustang GTD 1901—a special edition inspired by the car that helped launch Henry Ford's automotive empire.

According to recent reports, the Mustang GTD 1901 has a 789-horsepower advantage over the Sweepstakes car, but the design inspiration is clear. The Mustang GTD 1901 features a distinctive Royal Red exterior and a wide, off-center black racing stripe featuring a bright red centerline. The color combination reverses the original race car's black body and deep red chassis components. Additional diagonal graphics and exposed carbon-fiber elements, including the front splitter, rocker panels, rear diffuser, and wing, complete the exterior look.

Have a seat inside the Mustang GTD 1901, and you immediately realize this is not an ordinary GTD—that is, if there is even such a thing as an ordinary GTD. The first thing you notice are the Mahogany Red leather seats with Race Red stitching. Keep looking, and you’ll see there are also matching red accents on the seatbelts, while the steering wheel receives Mahogany Red faux suede.

The Performance Package is standard equipment on the Mustang GTD 1901. Options include the magnesium wheels, which reduce the unsprung weight by 50.3 pounds. If you want to spice up the interior, you can order the optional titanium trim package, which gets you redesigned titanium shifter paddles that have been lengthened for the 2028 model year. The titanium trim in the GTD, by the way? It comes from retired F-22 fighter jets.

Industry observers note that ford has not unveiled how many Mustang GTD 1901’s will be built, or how much they will cost. But we wouldn’t count on seeing too many at your local track day.

A lot has changed since Henry Ford won his first race; horsepower figures, aerodynamics, and suspension technology have come a long way. But the desire of the tech giant that bears his name to prove itself on the racetrack apparently hasn't changed much at all, and that’s something we’re certainly thankful for.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, residents of New Smyrna Beach, Florida, can finally breathe a sigh of relief.
  • According to the Volusia Sheriff’s Office, 75-year-old Robert Joseph Mitchell was riding his electric bicycle along the beach on November 13 when a sheriff’s deputy clocked him traveling 16 mph in a 10 mph zone (26 km/h in a 16 km/h zone).
  • The deputy attempted to stop Mitchell, who allegedly responded with a middle finger and some choice words before continuing on his way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, residents of New Smyrna Beach, Florida, can finally breathe a sigh of relief. A dangerous menace to society has been taken off the streets after police apprehended a 75-year-old man accused of leading deputies on a high-stakes electric bike chase at speeds reaching a blistering 16 mph (26 km/h).

According to the Volusia Sheriff’s Office, 75-year-old Robert Joseph Mitchell was riding his electric bicycle along the beach on November 13 when a sheriff’s deputy clocked him traveling 16 mph in a 10 mph zone (26 km/h in a 16 km/h zone).

The deputy attempted to stop Mitchell, who allegedly responded with a middle finger and some choice words before continuing on his way.

What followed was apparently the world’s slowest police chase.

According to recent reports, mitchell reportedly continued riding along the beach, eventually exiting onto city streets, where he allegedly rode against traffic before making it back to his home. Deputies followed him, and when Mitchell attempted to retreat into his garage, he reportedly resisted arrest by grabbing onto a golf cart and refusing to let go.

It has been revealed that the ordeal ended with Mitchell in custody, facing four charges, including felony fleeing or attempting to elude law enforcement, resisting an officer without violence, speeding on the beach, and riding outside the designated beach driving area. His bond was set at $4,000.

Sources indicate that and just like that, another dangerous electric bicycle criminal was brought to justice. This was clearly a success story like no other, and American streets are now safer.

Now, before anyone gets too worked up, let’s be clear: I’m not suggesting that e-bike riders should be allowed to ignore traffic laws, endanger pedestrians, or flee from police. Reports indicate that Mitchell was riding recklessly around beachgoers, including children, and that’s certainly something worth addressing. And once he allegedly decided to flee from deputies, he turned what could have been a minor infraction into a much more serious situation.

But can we also acknowledge how absurd this whole thing is?

We’ve reached a point where a 75-year-old man riding a bicycle at 16 mph can end up the subject of a police pursuit and felony charges, while we’ve largely accepted that multi-ton vehicles routinely kill and seriously injure people on our roads as an unavoidable cost of modern transportation.

Every day, drivers speed through neighborhoods, roll through stop signs, stare at their phones, and operate vehicles capable of killing pedestrians with a moment’s inattention. Or perhaps I shouldn’t say ‘capable’, but rather that they do. 40,000 people every year die in the US from car violence. Yet somehow, electric bicycles have become one of the great transportation menaces of our time, despite contributing much, much less to major bodily harm or death.

And yes, there are absolutely legitimate concerns about dangerous riding. I’ve repeatedly argued that we need better enforcement, especially when it comes to teenagers riding high-powered electric dirt bikes and e-motos at 40 mph (64 km/h) down sidewalks and bike paths. Those aren’t electric bicycles, and treating them as such has created a real problem for everyone.

But if we’re going to devote police resources to cracking down on dangerous two-wheeled behavior, perhaps we could start there instead of turning a 1 mph beach ride into the crime of the century.

What is absurd is that he didn't simply stop and follow the officer's directions to slow down. If he is going to try to flee from the police by riding dangerously including going against traffic then he should face charges. As presumably a first time offender, he'll be given probation if he agrees not to do it again.

To be fair, Mitchell’s alleged behavior after being stopped certainly didn’t help his case. But the larger point remains: our priorities around road safety have become wildly distorted.

We’ve normalized the dangers of cars so thoroughly that we barely blink at the daily carnage they cause, yet we’re increasingly treating comparatively low-speed electric bicycles as an existential threat to public safety.

Recent findings suggest that I’m all for enforcing sensible e-bike rules. I’m all for throwing the book at major infractions and scofflaws who pose a public menace. But I’m also for applying a little perspective.

Industry observers note that because if a 75-year-old man riding an electric bicycle at 16 mph is among our most pressing transportation safety concerns, then I have some very good news about the state of our roads. But unfortunately, there is no good news to share today.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that nesting season has officially begun for the seabirds visiting Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge near Hawaii. The first egg of the season was laid by a black-footed albatross (Phoebastria nigripes) or kaʻupu in Hawaiian. Field biologist and photographer Dan Rapp captured video of this exciting first, which Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge shared on social media.

Black-footed albatrosses are typically the first to lay eggs beginning in November. The Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis) or mōlī in Hawaiian, will lay their eggs in late November through December. Every fall, this remote group of islands about 1,250 miles from Honolulu temporarily becomes the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species, and includes the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any living bird species.

Sources indicate that one special albatross couple has already been spotted—George and Geraldine. The duo is together for the 10th straight year. George was first spotted exactly one month ago on October 18, and the couple was reunited by October 22. The pair are short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus) or makalena in Hawaiian. Short-tailed albatrosses can live up to 50 years and are monogamous—clearly.

Wisdom, a particularly famous bird in these parts, has not been spotted just yet. The over 70-year-old Laysan albatross is the oldest known banded wild bird in the world. She was first identified and banded in 1956 by wildlife biologist Chandler Robbins after she laid a single egg. Biologists estimate that she has produced 50 to 60 eggs and as many as 30 of her chicks have fledged in her lifetime. In 2024, Wisdom became the world’s oldest known wild bird to successfully lay an egg at the estimated age of 74. In March, she became a grandmother again.

Viewers can take in the sights and sounds of the albatross colony via live cameras and follow Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge for updates.

Viewers can expect to see the birds return to the islands, perform various courtship dances, begin to nest, lay their eggs, and eventually watch albatross chicks in all their fluffy glory.

Latest Update: Why the Most Politically Savvy Colleague Gets Things Done

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Updated November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • In a recent development, A department head needs budget for a project.
  • In a recent development, so in the week before the meeting, she has three separate conversations with people who will make or break the decision.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

In a recent development, A department head needs budget for a project. She knows the formal process: Write the proposal, present it at the monthly meeting, and then wait for feedback. She also knows how decisions are actually made in her organization.

In a recent development, so in the week before the meeting, she has three separate conversations with people who will make or break the decision. First, she talks with the finance director, who worries about cost overruns at the end of every quarter. Then, she talks with the operations head, whose team always gets dragged into projects that sometimes go nowhere. Next, she talks to the program lead who will "volunteer" to manage the project.

By the time she presents, the decision has effectively been made. People raise issues briefly as a formality because they already feel assured, and some even answer their own questions because they like the solution they were shown in advance.

Sources indicate that there are a couple of ways to look at this approach. It's definitely an effective approach. Some people would call it clever, but not everyone would mean that as a compliment.

It has been revealed that the resourceful style is one of the "dark side" personality styles: everyday patterns that can help or hinder us at work, depending on how strongly they show up and in what form. Its most extreme form resembles what psychologists call Machiavellianism, a cynical, self-serving approach to other people.

People who do this as a regular course of action share this way of viewing the world, navigating work through relationships, and many of them are transactional. They understand how power structures and networks truly exist in reality, separate from the official org chart or chain of command. They rapidly pick up on who makes decisions, or who suggests the ideas that get picked up more often than not.

They tend to be strategic, focused on outcomes, and can be very adaptable when the route to a goal changes or new obstacles emerge.

Researchers have studied the useful side of this for decades under the name "political skill." Ferris and colleagues (2005) developed a measure of it with four parts: social astuteness (reading people and situations), interpersonal influence, networking ability, and apparent sincerity (coming across as genuine).

Industry observers note that A meta-analysis by Munyon and colleagues (2015) found that political skill was linked to higher productivity, career success, a better reputation, and greater job satisfaction. It predicted task performance even after accounting for broad personality traits and general intelligence.

According to recent reports, when the researchers looked at the four aspects separately, networking, influence, and apparent sincerity predicted performance. Social astuteness on its own did not. Reading the room is a useful start, but the rarer skill is reading a room and influencing your place in it.

Recent findings suggest that at their best, resourceful people do exactly that. They get around obstacles that stall everyone else, and find the person who can make a decision or make the obstacles go away. They can get other people to support them to make unpopular decisions, and if they get the desired results, some people will respect and admire them for it.

According to recent reports, this can be done proactively and prosocially, or in ways that are counterproductive and manipulative. Organizations and even small teams are political whether or not anyone likes it, and someone who can find ways of making things work is necessary for any high-functioning team.

The dark side emerges when people become collateral damage. Consider a colleague who builds trust with a peer during a brutal restructuring, learns that the peer is burned out and looking for another job, and later uses that confidence to edge them out of a key role when budgets tighten.

As I discussed in a post on destructive behavior in the remote office, a manipulative person can work this way with surgical precision, especially when much of the work happens across different and poorly organized communication channels.

It has been revealed that however, it is possible to operate in some gray areas while still maintaining respectful and mutually beneficial relationships. Arguably, it's a more successful strategy in the longer term.

The research on Machiavellianism shows the cost of being too ruthless. A meta-analysis by O'Boyle and colleagues (2012) found it was linked to more counterproductive work behavior, meaning behavior that harms colleagues or the organization. Its link to lower job performance was small and inconsistent, which fits the idea that this style can deliver short-term results while eroding the reliability and trust that long-term work requires.

It helps to compare this style with more combative, rule-breaking tendencies that are compulsive instead of calculated. Combative people tend to push boundaries, take visible risks, and ask forgiveness rather than permission. Resourceful people usually leave the rules intact and work the system instead. They do not need to skip the approval process when they have already lined up the approvers.

That can make the resourceful style harder to spot, and its destructive form harder to challenge. Nothing improper has technically happened. The damage is a loss of trust amongst teams.

As I argued in "The Surprising Upside of Your Dark Side," the question to ask of personality styles is: How do you use them?

People who read power well will always have an advantage in certain types of work. Whether others experience them as a valuable ally or a threat depends less on how well they play the game than on what they are trying to accomplish.

In a recent development, macRae, I. (2022). Dark social: Understanding the darker side of work, personality and social media. Bloomsbury.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you wake up tomorrow as the esteemed Lord Mayor of London, you’ll want to make a properly dignified entrance. To make sure your arrival turns the right heads, Electrogenic has taken the Mayor’s 1973 Roll-Royce Phantom VI and turned it into a properly traditional standard-bearer with modern electric power.

The stately, stylish, and silent electric Rolls-Royce car made its public debut at last month’s Salon Privé weekend at Blenheim Palace, where it joined a growing fleet of classic Rollers that have received Elctrogenic’s electric conversion, including the stunning Mulliner-bodied 1929 Phantom II that we covered back in 2023.

Recent findings suggest that for this project, Electrogenic carefully removed the internal combustion-based engine, transmission, and fuel system from the City of London Corporation’s official ’73 Phantom VI limo and replaced it with a 120 kW (~160 hp) electric motor putting out 310 Nm (~230 lb-ft) of torque. Sharp-eyed readers will note those numbers are significantly lower than what you’d expect from the 6.2L L410 V8 fitted with twin SU carburetors (as it was in the standard ’73 IV), but since those numbers were never officially published, we would say that the power available from the new electric drivetrain is similarly adequate for Mayoral use.

Power for the electric motor comes from a 62 kWh li-ion battery fitted under the hood bonnet, and offers more than enough range to get the Lord Mayor to their appointments in and around the city.

To ensure the heads of the heads of the city don’t bob in an undignified manner while on parade, Electrogenic added a “ceremonial” drive mode that trims power and torque and softens the throttle map, so the chauffeur can more easily hold the crawling pace demanded by civic processions and state occasions.

According to recent reports, “We were honored to be asked to electrify this significant motor car, and to play a part in the City of London Corporation’s journey to net zero,” says Steve Drummond, chief executive of Electrogenic. “When it was introduced in the late 1960s, the Rolls-Royce VI was the most refined and dignified limousine on the road. Now, thanks to electrification, its core character has been enhanced further: it is whisper quiet, effortless to drive with swift performance, and emits zero tailpipe emissions.”.

It's notable for government to be seen to follow it's own policy.

A standard complaint by oil lobbyists is that government vehicles aren't electrified.

Only 374 Phantom VIs were built between 1968 and 1990, with this 3 meter-long coach-built limousine having been commissioned during the mayoralty of Alderwoman Dame Susan Langley DBE, the 697th Lord Mayor of the City of London. The Phantom was converted as part of the Corporation’s broader effort to achieve a net zero carbon emissions goal from its own operations in 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that on Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters.
  • Officials blueprint to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone.
  • Industry observers note that the aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters. This time, the alert is targeting a much different kind of public threat: sneaky standardized test cheaters.

Officials blueprint to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone. Proctors will also inspect all pairs of glasses for hidden cameras, and students wearing clothes with buttons will have to cover them with stickers.

Industry observers note that the aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score. That surprise revelation sent educators and officials scrambling to come up with solutions to instill confidence in the upcoming test.

In a recent development, korea’s measures come as educators around the world are struggling to keep up with a growing arsenal of AI-enabled tools that make cheating easier than ever. But while AI is the focus today, students have been tinkering with upcoming tech and other creative ways to skirt the rules for as long as tests have carried weight.

It has been revealed that the sudden rule changes in South Korea come days after a 34-year-old man named Han Won-seok posted a video on his lawyer’s YouTube channel admitting he used AI to cheat on the country’s national tax exam. According to the Associated Press, Han scored 397.5 out of 400 points on the first stage of the multiple-choice test, a suspicious result that made him the subject of several media interviews. Other test-takers saw those results and accused him of trickery.

It has been revealed that days after denying those allegations, Han reversed course. In the video, he admitted to using a miniature camera to photograph the exam questions, which were then fed to an AI tool. He then viewed the AI-generated answers on his smartphone. Now, Han states he is cooperating with investigators and is warning others against following his lead.

“I cheated on the tax accountant exam. I sincerely apologize for causing damage to a lot of people,” the student mentioned in the video, according to CNN. “If there is someone thinking of cheating like I did, I’m going to tell the investigators everything, so I hope you don’t think that you won’t get caught.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the days since the videos, officials have rushed to put in place latest anti-cheating safeguards. South Korean Prime Minister Han Sung-sook reportedly held a meeting on Monday with the country’s top education officials, where they agreed to officially add smart glasses to the list of prohibited items in testing rooms. Some lawmakers had reportedly even called on officials to postpone the Suneung exam until they could come up with more rigorous anti-cheating safeguards, though the country’s Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin promptly shot that idea down, arguing delays would cause “even a larger disruption.” And while Han never said he specifically used smart glasses to cheat, worries about that tech in particular aren’t hypothetical. Earlier this year, two other South Korean students taking an exam to assess English skills were also caught using camera-equipped glasses.

In a recent development, concerns about AI-enabled cheating aren’t limited to South Korea either. Last week, England’s Office for Students, an independent higher education regulator, released a statement warning that AI tools are making it “close to impossible” to assess university classwork. In China, major tech companies disabled features on their AI apps during last year’s national college entrance exam (the gaokao), to keep students from using them to cheat. Educators in the United States and elsewhere are also increasingly requiring students to take exams in person and defend papers orally due to the pervasiveness of AI-generated submissions. Sales of Blue Books have soared as a result.

Sources indicate that while fancy AI tools and camera-equipped smart glasses may be latest concerns, creative cheating isn’t. In fact, evidence of sneaky test-takers dates back centuries. One example is this replica of a linen vest from China’s Qing dynasty (1644–1911). The impressive garment has 62 essays, more than 40,000 characters in all, hidden inside. Students wearing the vest would sneak peeks during the country’s grueling imperial exams, which played an crucial role in determining government employment and social status. An even older Ming Dynasty (1368 to 1644) jacket was covered with some 50,000 characters from classical texts likely served a similar purpose.

It has been revealed that creative cheating has of course persisted into the modern era. In 2015, police in India’s Bihar state detained more than 1,000 people after relatives of test-takers were photographed scaling the walls of an exam center to pass cheat sheets to students through a window opening. A college student in the U.S. made headlines in 2011, after he was arrested for allegedly using fake IDs to stand in for at least six high school students during SAT exams. In China, a team of exam proctors equipped with  surveillance drones regularly seizes a variety of wearables and other devices students use to try and cheat. Among the seized items were a hidden camera placed inside a pen and glasses with cameras connected to a tiny receiver embedded in a coin.

One has to wonder if all that time and effort spent devising intricate cheating methods could have been used to study instead.
